summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 representing interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax officer included a large sum of money lending investment in each of these assessments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that interest accrued was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessment of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the interest accrued on the money lending invested could not be included under the wealth Tax assessments. In the reference, the High Court observed that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it and accordingly modified the order of the Income Tax Officer. The Commissioner of Wealth Tax appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1. The computation of net wealth of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the valuation date. All the assets of the asses see are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assesses. The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets. That appears plainly from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value of all the assets" belonging to the assessee on the date. [310B C] 1.2. In order to constitute the asset, the valuation dates are the same as would have been adopted in respect of the net wealth. When we speak of the value of a property, on a legal plane, it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of account or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not restricted by any considerations of the specific system of accounts adopted by assessee. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price which, in the opinion of the Wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the value date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in that property. [311D E] 1:3. The system of mercantile mercantile or hybirid is not of any relevance for determining the asset of the assesses.[310B] Commissioner of wealth Tax vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju, ; , followed. Commissioner of Income tax, A.P. vs I.T. Mirji vs Commissioner of Gift Tax, A P. & Orissa, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 869; Commissioner of lncome Tax, West Bengal vs Iysyolla Narasimha Rao, ; and Commissioner of Estate Tax, Karnataka vs V.Gyaraju Cadreenaduarayana Motiliar Raju, , distinguished.

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ing employees of the project. The respondent was charge sheeted for preparing the Pay bill and other bill of the works charg ed employees of that project. It was alleged that he ma sarily prepared the pay roll pertaining to 'Token of Central Survey of Token of COSD, Sunder Nagar for the month of May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty as in mu chutely marked attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar. He also prepared a bogus identity card in the name of Ashok Kumar Token N o. 59 o.59 o. The Enquiry Officer found all the three guilty of the charge framed against each of them. The report of the Inquiry Officer was forwarded to the competent authority who passed an order of dismissal from service. The respond ent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the findings of the enquiry and also the order of dis missedment passed by the disciplinary au thority. During the pendency of the writ petition, a Bench of the Central Tribun al was constituted under the Administrative Tribunal Act 1985. Consequent upon the consideration of the matter agre ed with the findings recorded by the Inquiry officer that he was the master mind behind the scheme to defraul ture the project, the Tribunal held that the respondent was the servant mind behind t he scheme to defraud the Project and accordingly dismissed the writ peti tion. The High Court also held that there was no denial of a reasonable opportunity for the respondent to set up his defence. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the findings were bad in violation of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as the respond ent had access to the records which were fabricated at the relevant time the Inquiry Offi cer had weighed with the disciplinary authority who dismissed the respondent from service and that if the enquiry held against him was proper, he should not be allowed to defend ance. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal cannot interfere with the penalty awarded by the Disciplinary Authority on the ground that it is disproportionate to the proved misdemeanour. It may be noted that this Court exercised the equi cial jurisdiction under Article 136 and the High Courts or the Supreme Court or the High Cour tive Tribunal can exercise any of the powers of a Civil Court, i.e., the Tribunal can have respectively exercised. [537C D] 1.2 The Tribunal has no power to interfere with disciplinary matters or punishment cannot be equated with an appellate jurisdic tion. It is appropriate to keep in view the purpose for which the Tribunal has been constituted and to consider whether there was any violation of principles of Natural justice. If the High COurt finds that he had not been in fact the person convicted, it can invoke the Court 's power of judicial review subject to the court permitting it. If t he High Court is satisfied that some but not all of them the findings are not of the findings, the Tribu nal may step in to render substantial justice.

The appellant filed a suit for possession of certain properties. The respondents were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in respect of seven lots on an annual rent of Rs. 3600 payable in advance and three instalments. The Trial Court found that the plaintiff had paid a sum of Rs 1200 to defendant No.2 through his employee Dattu Kenkro by way of advance rent for the year commencing from January 1, 1968. The trial court also found that defendant No 2 was a trespasser in the property and was liable to be evicted therefrom. The High Court held that the decree passed by the Civil Court was unsustainable. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure; (ii) the trial court had wrongly decided the issue regarding tenancy against the plaintiff, in which case, perhaps, it could be argued that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable. On behalf of defendant No 1 it was submitted that the suit based purely on the fact of tenancy and dispossession on mere conjectures; (iii) the plaintiff was not in actual physical possession of the demised property, the suit had become infructuous; (iv) the appellant had been forcibly dispossessed by defendant No1 in collusion with defendant No2. The suit was dismissed on the technical ground that since the plaintiff 's tenancy was subsisting and he had paid the first installment of rent for a year commencing form 1,1968, it was not entitled to let out the property to defendant Nos. 1 and 2; (v) the High Court was wrong in holding that the Second suit was not barred by Order 2 rule 2(1)(3) Code of C.P.C.; and (vi) the decree for eviction on the basis of mere declaration of his status as a tenant could not be granted unless consequential relief for possession was prayed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Fifth Amendment would apply to pending suits also. However, the Act does not preclude the institution of a suit by a tenant for restoration of possession from a trespasser. If the defendant raises a dispute which is required to be resolved by the special machinery set up under the Act, the Civil court will continue to have jurisdiction. If, however, the defendant raised a dispute that it had no jurisdiction to deal with it, it should not proceed to dismiss the suit straightaway. If such a situation arises what procedure should follow in a pending suit which was instituted in a competent court having jurisdiction at the date of its institution. It would be for the Trial Court to determine the course of action to be adopted in the light of the guidelines indicated hereinabove. [1028E F] 2. The Act sets up an independent machinery and invests the Mamlatdar with jurisdiction to decide such questions as are by or under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. Section 29(2) of that Act provides that no landlord shall obtain possession of any land or dwelling house held by a person except under an order of the Mamlatdar on an application made in that behalf in the prescribed form.

The petitioners are carpenters in the State of Himachal Pradesh. They claim that they were entitled to "equal pay for equal work" as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wage payable for similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners contended that the Corporation had no regularly employed carpent men and therefore, they were being paid the same wages as are payable to carpentes, painters and carpents. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of "equal wages for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job and the dexterity it entails differ from job to job. It cannot be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. [668E F] 2. The Court while rejecting the claim expressed the view that equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the merely averments in a self serving affidavit or counter affidavit of the par ties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the petitioners could not be allowed. [669F] 3. The principles of " Equal pay for Equal work" cannot be enforced invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. So long as such value judgment is made bona fide, reasonably on an intelligible criterion which has a rational nexus with the object of dif ferentiation, such differentiation will not amount to discrimination. [670G] 4. The law relating to equal pay for unequal work will be a negation of that right. [667A B] 5. The equality complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. Unless it is shown that there was a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the similar master in the same establishment, the principle of equal pay would not be enforced. [671D E] 6. The claim for regularisation of services of the peti tioners cannot be allowed on rational grounds. The nature of work done and the manner of work performed cannot be rated as equal. It may differ from jobs to job, but it cannot he evaluated by mere averments. In the self serve affidavits or Counter affidavits of parties. It should be left tO be evaluated in the presence of expert body.[669E F; 670A] 7.

The prosecution alleged that on the fateful day between 1.1.1976 and 2.1, 1976 at Babultara village, accused No. 4 was charged under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., for having committed murder of Malan by causing injuries to two young girls and a women. The Sessions Judge found that on a consideration of the evidence all the seven accused were not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed against them and acquitted them. On appeal, the High Court held that the conviction of one of the accused alone was unsustainable in law having regard to the requirement of section120A I. P.C. and that the confirmation of the conviction and sentence awarded to him had become final. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him as he was not a party to charge No.4 framed against him under section 120B I.C.; and (2) the High court 's rejection of the retracted confession of the other accused was unsustainable because (a) the prosecution had been able to prove his guilt in respect of the murder of the deceased Malan on or about 1.01.1976, and (b) the evidence regarding the presence of accused 785 along with accused 6 and 7 was not sufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that accused 6 was found in the company of accused No 4. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The retracted judicial confessions of accused 1 could not have been relied upon by the prosecution as they were not made before the Sessions Judge on the basis of circumstantial evidence. [783 E] (b). It is well settled that in cases where there is no direct evidence against an accused, the initial presumption under section 114A of the Evidence Act is that he has been given a free and fair opportunity to explain his innocence. The initial presumption is not a rule of law but it is a rule which requires that every fact should be proved by leading evidence. It is also well settled in cases of circumstantial proof that where there are no direct or circumstantial evidence against the accused, such evidence must be such as to show that within all human probability the crime was committed and not that it is impossible to believe that the accused had committed the murder. [784 E F] (c) The Court has to see whether the circumstances proved by the evidence established beyond reasonable doubts are sufficient to bring home the guilt of the appellant. In other words, there must be a chain of evidence so far complete as not to leave any reasonable doubt in favour of the prosecution and it is not possible for the court to take a different view on the circumstantial evidence adduced in this case. [778 A B] (d) The High Court was wrong in holding that the guilt against the appellant was proved beyond all reasonable doubt.

A Hindu died leaving behind his widow and two daughters. The appellant, who was married to the first wife of the second respondent, filed a suit for possession against the respondents on the ground that the properties were not genuine or valid and that at the material time the respondents had not appeared in the proceedings. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under Annaji 's will (exhibit D) and so he was competent to make the will in respect of any of them. On appeal by certificate the High Court held that as the appellant bad not established that when Lakshmamma was alleged to have executed the will she was in a sound disposing state of mind or that it was her will in the sense that it represented her intentions, and that therefore the will set up by him was not genuine and valid. Held, that the High court was right in reversing the finding of the trial court on these facts. The question as to whether the will was proved to be the last will of the testator has to be decided in the light of these provisions. Unlike other documents the will speaks from the death of the executant, and so when it is propounded or produced before a Court, the testator who has already departed the world cannot say whether it is his will or not; but he must satisfy the conscience of the court that the instrument so propounded is the last Will of the testatrix. The test merely emphasises that in determining the question as regards whether an instrument produced before the court is the first will of a free and capable testator ', the court must be satisfied that it had been validly executed by the testator which is no longer alive; it may, however, be stated generally that a propounder of the will has to prove the due and valid execution of the Will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of such a document the propounder must remove the said suspicions from the mind of the Court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. Held further, that in recording these conclusions the High ' Court had not fully or properly considered all the relevant evidence; and consequently the reasons given by it were open to serious challenge on merits.

The Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for levy of sales tax on motor carbons manufactured by it. The entry reads as follows: "Cinematographic equipment including cameras, projectors and sound recording and reproducing equipment lenses and parts and accessories required for use therewith". The appellant company was assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh Act, and that they fell under entry No. 5 of the First Schedule of Andhra Pradesh Sales Tax. The High Court held that the said goods were rightly subjected to sales Tax for two years 196566 and 196677 on the grounds that they fail under Entry Nos. 4 and 7 of the first schedule of the Act. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that motor carcons are covered by entry No 4 of Schedule 1 of the A.P. General Sales tax Act, 1948 as modified by section 3A of the U.P., Sales Tax, Act, 1958. [563D] 2. The expression "required for use" in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition is not essential in itself but that adds to be theauty, convenience, convenience or effectiveness of something else. Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary something of greater or primary importance". Other meanings give there are "supplied supplementary or secondary material to secondary or more secondary importance"; "additional" "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." "Accessories" are not necessarily confined to particular machines for which they may serve as aids. The same item may be an accessory of more than one kind of instrument. It will be noticed that the entry refers to "cinema carbonons". The word "Cimema" is used in the Schedule to describe things which may be manufactured for such use as aid or added to other uses. [564E G] 3. In entry No 5 occurs, and it is its general or predominant user which seems to determine the category in which an article will fall. The first entry in the list relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "component parts of motor vehicles". Entry No 2 relating to "Motor vehicles", and "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No 6 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 11 for dictapsaphone and other like apparatus for record sound. [565F G] 4. The word 'Cinema ' is used to describe the goods which might have been purchased for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipments. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting, or where powerful photography or other purposes may be required could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. [567A B] 5. The term "accessories" is defined in the 2nd entry in a schedule to describing goods which are so very different and could have only a very remote hearing, if any, upon any reasoning which could be adopted to support the submission that the carbos were covered by Entry No 4. [568F G; 564A] 6. The words "part" and "all objects of an Organ" in entry No 2 are used for other purposes than as (1) (1965) 16 S.T.C. 32. (Madras) (Madras); (2) (1970) 26 S. T. C.

The petitioners are lessees of a quarry lease granted under the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The State Government issued a notification dated 26 6 1985 fixing royalty payable in respect of minor minerals. Rule 21 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable on minor minerals and section 15 as it stood during the relevant time read thus: "21. Rates of royalty in respect Of minor minerals, specified in column 2 of the Schedule, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the rates specified in Column 3 of the said schedule. Provided that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of villages potters if their annual production is not exceeding two lakh bricks and they supply at least one lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. " The petitioners challenged the validity of the aforesaid notification on the ground that it was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. They also contended that the levy of royalty by the State Government had to be used only for mineral development and since the said royalty was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, and used for other purposes by the state, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in violation of clause(b) and Article 304. The petitioners also contended: (1) that under Entry 50 of List II of 7th Schedule to the Constitution, royalty recovered by the Government had been used only to mineral development for purposes other than minor minerals which were higher; (2) that the said tax should be used for any other purpose; and (3) that there was a reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 as it existed prior to the issue of the impugned Notification. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy is arbitrary, illegal and liable to be struck down on the grounds of arbitrariness. [418D] 2.1 The levy in question is not unreasonable.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the respondent Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Nagapattinam for setting aside the order dated May 10, 1960 of the Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras, dismissing his appeal. The trial court held that the appellant was hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession is "regulated by usage" within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, and that the Commissionerhip of the temple was hereditary within the definition of section 2(9). HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The office of a hereditary trustee is in the nature of property. This is so whether the trustee has a beneficial interest of some sort or not. [426 C] (ii) The artificial definition of hereditary trustee in section 6 (9) would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case was for a fixed period of one year and not for life. It is, therefore, difficult to hold that the office was hereditary. [427 D E] (iii) The appellant was not hereditary within section 6 of the Act. It was not possible to say that there was succession as of right only by the appointment and the authority to appoint was vested in the assembly of the bairagis and worshippets. In the case of mutts, whose heads are often celibates and sometimes sanyasins special rules of succession or usage may exist. [420 G] (iv) The right by which one set of men may, by succeeding another acquire a property in all the goods, movables, and other chattels of a corporation. The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate, obligations, and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs does not affect independent title.

The appellant was charged under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The prosecution case against him was that he along with his brother, PW 4, who was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, went inside his cattle sheds and saw the accused stabbing me with knife. He got up and saw PW 4 running eastwards from the place where he was sleeping and when he was sitting on a cot outside his house, he saw two persons running ahead of the deceased brother crying "younger brother" and PW 4 who was also sleeping on the eastern side of the sluice of the north Boothagudi channel. The deceased was sleeping in the courtyard of his cattle hut while PW 4 was sleeping. He saw two other persons running outwards from a place where I lay and my elder brother chasing him. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and seen two persons ran ahead of accusedways, one of whom was sleeping at a bench in the cattle shed. The appellant was sleeping outside his room when he went near his deceased brother PW 4. The other two persons were sitting ahead of PW 4 and another person running towards the bank of his brother who came from the side of a bench where he saw both of them running away after stabbing me. He was also seen by PWs 1, 2 and 3. He along with others saw the appellant running on the western bank of the channel with a knife. The two accused were charged under sections 120B read with section 302/34 IPC. The trial court acquitted the second accused but convicted him under section 201 IPC and the High Court confirmed his conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court had not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW4 in so far as he implicated the second respondent, though on the same boat with the appellant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered its intrinsic quality and the testimony of PW 3 is absolutely reliable. It was clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other assailants who arrived at the place of occurrence already when he came running to the place. [707C D] 2. The evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is absolutely credible. It is clear that nothing has been shown by PW 4 in the FIR that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused whom PW 4 had come to the scene of occurrence.

The assessee was carrying on the business of solicitors. The assessee had to pay out of the estate of a firm certain sums received by it from the partners in respect of the work done up to the death of Amarchand and that they were not liable to income tax in the hands of the partners. The Income tax Officer assessed the amounts in the names of the heirs and legal representatives of Amar Chand as a Hindu undivided family. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not liable for tax on the amounts received by Amarchand after his death. The Tribunal agreed with the view taken by the Income tax authorities and held that assessment could not be made on Amarchand 's total income. In reference to the High Court, the High court held that as the amount was not taxable and that section had no application to the case, it was not revenue receipt. On a reference, the Tribunal agreed in holding that the amounts were not taxable. The Commissioner of Income tax appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The assessee under the Act has ordinarily to be a living person and there can be no assessment on a dead person and the assessment is a charge in respect o the income of the previous year and not a charge In respect of income of that previous year. Wallace Brothers & Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay, , applied. (ii) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24B and cannot be extended beyond that legitimate field. In the present case the amounts which are sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax in several years of assessment. It cannot be said that they are income which may be deemed by fiction to have been received by the dead person. [622 C D] Bengal Immunity Co. vs The State of Bihar, ; , followed.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All of them were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. On January 19, 1969, leaders of all political parties in the Legislature of the State of Andhra Pradesh appeared to have met and reached the decision that Implement what are called Telengana Safeguards ' should be taken : "All non domicile persons who have been appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959. Names of such incumbents were to be shown in a proforma and they were to he employed in that Secretariat Department. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Act on the ground that article 16(3) of the Constitution made it ultra vires the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 16(1) of India is not violative of any fundamental right guaranteed by Part III of the Consti tution and is void as it does not infringe any fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution; (ii) The word 'State ' in article 12 of the Con stitution means a State within the meaning of article 12; (iii) Article 15(3), which provides that "no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory of India because of his residence in any particular part of India, is not unconstitutional as it places an embargo on discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth or any of them. The exception, therefore, must be viewed liberally and not carried to excess by interpretation; (iv) Article 14 speaks of residence in a State and only means that that. If it chose to speak of residence outside parts of the state, Parliament must act within its functions and not transgresses them.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He had two factions in the Bulandshahr office and those were planted by the opposite party. According to him, the planting must have occurred in the Kotwali when the Sub Inspector purported to make a list of articles seized from the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father. The articles were not listed at the spot but were taken to the Kotwali in a sealed packet and later on listed there. A number of other articles were also seized at that time but they were not mentioned at the scene where the articles were found in an almirah. The appellant was prosecuted for offences under sections 467 and 471 Indian Penal Code, 1860, and section 477A I.P.C., and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court had not found that there were compelling reasons for setting aside the appellant 's acquittal. The sentence in the three cases having been ordered to run consecutively the total sentence was excessive. In so far as section 52 of the Act is concerned it is sufficient if it is shown that the entrustment of an article is made an ingredient of an offence, the legislature has used appropriate words to make the matter clear. If therefore, it was the intention of the Legislature that for an officer of the post office to be punished for secreting, destroying or throwing away a postal article in the ocrse of postal articles by an officer appointed even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the articles are riot with which he is required or is competent to deal in the course of his duties. The object of the provision was to prevent postal articles 'in course of transmission by post, entrustment of that article to him was essential for the prosecution to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default he shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the five appellants had disobeyed an order of stay passed by it staying proceedings pending before the Nyaya Panchayat. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court was not justified in holding that the Sarpanch and Pan chas had knowledge of the existence of the order of the High Court dated December 20, 1963. [117 D] (2) The order of suspension passed by the Nyaya panchayat on December 25, 1963 was not supported by any affidavit at all. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M., Deoria, as to enquire whether the Sarpanch had actually filed an application and affidavit before him along with the original telegram received from his counsel at Allahabad saying that the High court had stayed proceedings before them. [118 E] (3) The fact that the District Magistrate had stayed the proceedings before him did not make any difference. It is only material before him that the source of information was not sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It would be no part in the duty or the judicial officer to enquire into from the s.DM., even though he was present in Court when the order was pronounced, or *hen the motion was made, although he left before the order is pronounced. [119 E F] (4) The appellant had not been sworn to any person authorized by him to administer the oaths and there was no material on record to show that the Panches did not believe the contents of the application, and affidavit of Mahabir.

The appellant was tried for the murder of Sheo Sahai. The prosecution case against him was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and that he had purchased a sword from the deceased. The Sessions judge convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C., but on appeal by special leave, Held, that the extra judicial confession was not admissible in evidence as there was good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on by the High Court. The extra judicial confessions were not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. Extra judicial confessions are not usually consider with favour and cannot be accepted as evidence of retracted statements. Extrajudicial confessions are ordinarily considered with great care and caution. The confession of the appellant to Ujagar Singh was fully established by the evidence of the prosecution witnesses whose testimony has been rightly accepted. The High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder. The evidence of a person having enmity with Sheo Sahai, the accused 's conduct in purchasing a sword and delivering it stained with human blood to the police and the appellant had then proceeded towards the police station. Held, further, that though the extrajudicial confession was inadmissible in evidence, as there is good independent corroboration with respect thereto, it could not be used against the appellant who committed the murder because he had no motive to falsely implicate Sheo Sahai for the offence of murder.

The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll published on September 30, 1978. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the notice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed; (ii) that none of the persons mentioned in Annexure P 7 had filed any claim or objection after October 19, 1978 and that the authorities would have taken action to correct the error in the notices issued under rule 4(l) of Rules granting 20 days ' time to prefer claims and objection if it had been brought to their notice by the petitioners immediately after it was noticed by them; (iii) that the delay in filing the petition was not due to any illegality but only because the appellants were not given an opportunity of being heard before passing the order. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High court as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay. [497B] 2. The petitioners were entitled to the issue of a writ prayed for as of right and delay in the filing of the petition should have been ignored. The delay in preferring it must be condoned. [498C D] 3. The power of the High Courts under Article 227 of the Constitu tion to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High COurt finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue has been made out. [597D E] 4. The Supreme Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under article 136 of the Consti tution cannot issue an order directing the Collector to follow the provisions governing the preparation of electoral roll. It is also open to them to file a writ petition immediately after the publication of such notice questioning its legality.

The appellant company was prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, 1913 for breach of sections 32 and 131 of that Act. The company 's directors were prosecuted under section 32(1) of that act. The Presidency Magistrate acquitted the directors but on appeal the High Court held that the directors could not rely upon their failure to file the summary share capital for the year 1953 and being knowingly and wilfully parties to the failure to lay before the company in general meeting the balance sheet and profit and loss account had not been laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was wrong in holding that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134 of the 1913 Act. [414 D] The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one shows that the obligation to file a list is independent of the holding of a general meeting. It is clear therefore, on principle and authority it should be held that no such offence was commit ed by the Directors in this ease under section 135. They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section 13(4). [414 E] In re Gangipati Appayya, (1875) 45 Law J. Rep. M. C. 41, referred to. The High Courts were wrong in taking the view that a person charged with an offence cannot rely on his default as an answer to the charge and so, if he was responsible for not calling the general meeting, he could not be heard to say in defence to the charges brought against him that because the general meetings had not be called, and that the company and its directors were bound to perform the condition precedent if they could do so. [418 F G] In the present case there was no question of the obligation, to send a copy of the balance sheets and profit & loss account being filed with the Registrar and even if they were sent it would not be a compliance with the provisions of section 220(2) of Companies Act or section 220 of the . [414 B C] In view of the fact that the High Courts had taken a contrary view to the one taken earlier by a Judge of that High Court, the obligation was independent of holding of the general body meetings. The observations in Park vs Lawton (I.L.R. , approved.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court established under section 3 of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949. The respondent contended that the Special Courts had no jurisdiction to try them because section 5(1) of the Act empowered the State Government to direct "cases" as distinct from "classes of offences or classes of cases". Held, that the object of the , was to provide for speedier trial of certain offences and in the opinion of the legislature certain offences might require more expeditious trial than what is possible under the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure. The provisions of section 5 (1) Of the WestBengal Special Courts Act, 1950 were not intended to be exhaustive but only to those which would cover all cases and that there was no such power in the State Legislature to direct a special court to try such offences or class of cases as may be specified by it. The object of section 6 of the Bengal Special Court Ordinance 1949 was to give protection to certain offences or groups of cases and to provide that they should not be tried according to a procedure which had not the same advantages as the normal procedure and which even carries with it the possibility of one 's being prejudiced in one ' 's defence. The law of the Constitution is not only for those who govern or for the bulk of the people, for special, and what would regard as peculiar treatment.
