The workmen of the appellant company were referred by the State Government under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items of dispute. The workmen raised a preliminary objection that the Tribunal was not justified in making the calculation at the minimum wages and that the High Court should have proceeded to make the alternative calculation on some other basis so as to arrive at a lower figure of Rs. 73 p.m. as production bonus. The appellant company contended before this Court that the proportion should be 3: 1: 1; that the workmen were not comparable with the Company, and that, in any case, the Tribunal had committed an error inasmuch as in making calculation the minimum wage was fixed for the Price Index instead of permitting neutralisation to the extent of at least 90%, which could have been done when fixing the minimum Wages being paid in those industries. Held: (i) The Tribunal committed no error of law requiring interference by this Court, in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. (ii) The Industrial Tribunal had the discretion to fix the minimum rate of wages that should ordinarily be adopted for the wage packet and it was not necessary that the minimum Wage should have been fixed by the tribunal which was being varied by the High court. (iii) The workmen were entitled to bonus on the same basis as the permanent workers for whom the minimum payment was fixed by this Tribunal. (iv) The award of the Tribunal did not violate any principles of natural justice requiring interference, because, it had to be kept in view that since then there has been a very considerable rise in the Price index and the labour had not so far raised a fresh dispute for a further revision of wages over and above the wages fixed by it. (v) The fact that the revised wages were payable with effect from 13th December 1962, was not conclusive as to whether the workmen should be allowed bonus on that basis. (vi) The payment of bonus in addition to the minimum pay in those concerns was made at least by the time when the award was given by the Industrial Tribunal and not before the expiry of the year 1962 63.

The assessee was a partnership firm. For the assessment year 1960 61, relevant to the accounting year 1959 60, the Income tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, and after obtaining the necessary satisfaction of the Commissioner of Income Tax, Bihar and Orissa, Patna, issued a notice under s 148 of that Act. The assessee challenged the validity of that notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notices on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act, and that the Commissioner had mechanically accorded permission. HELD : (i) The assessee 's omission to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for the accounting years in question, chargeable income tax had escaped assessment for that year. [466C] (ii) The order sheet recording the reasons of the Income Tax Officer as required by section 148(2), does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit case for issue of notice under Section 148. From the report submitted by the Incometax Officer to the Commissioner, it is clear that he could not have issued a show cause notice under S 148. [427D] (iii) The material that he had before him for issuing the notice under Sec. 148 was not mentioned in the report. In his report the Income ' tax Officer did not set out any reason as to why he should not have passed a notice. He did not record himself that he was satisfied that this was a fit one for issue.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in Calicut and Madras, was carrying on the business of manufacturing soap and yarn. In 1942, the firm consisted of Nagjee, Narayanjee and Manecklal. The firm consisted mainly of Nagji, Narayanji, Ramanujam and Co., and in the manufacture and sale of soap and umbrella manufacturers and sellers. The question for decision by the Tribunal was whether the appellant was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922, as amended in 1939. Held: (i) that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, as it then stood, and not under the fourth sub section of section 25 (4). The business must be carried on by a person different from those who carried on it on April 1, 1939. The partnership in question was dissolved in 1943 and the firm was reconstituted by an agreement of partnership dated December 6, 1918. It was not in existence in 1948 so as to permit a succession to it taking place under the instrument of February 7, 1948. (ii) that there was no succession within the meaning of section 26(2) of Act XLII of 1922 and the family was entitled only to the benefit mentioned in section 25. The business could be said to have taken place before the benefit of section 23(4). But it must be remembered that under section 2(1)(c), a mere change in the constitution of a firm or where a firm has been newly constituted and the second sub section, where there is a succession by another person for the purpose of section 27(2), does not necessarily bring into existence a new assessable unit or a distinct assessable entity. (iii) that under the law also there was a succession within section 25 to which the provisions of section 2 must be applied and in respect of which it must he considered whether there was such a succession, it is only one entity to which section 23 applies and in other cases, there is no devolution of the business as a whole. (iv) that section 25 expressly mentioned that a case of succession was not to be found where there was mere change of the constitution or the partnership without there being a succession. It is only when there was an discontinuance of the previous business before 1948 or a succession not amounting to a mere alteration in the Constitution of the firm, assessment has to be made under section 26 (2).

The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the plaintiff 's suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that the properties were Khandappa 's self acquisitions and that on a true view of law, the widow 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husbands 's interest upon his death. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the suit property belonged to a joint family consisting only of her father, wife and their children; (ii) the widow and daughter were amongst the female relatives specified in class I of the Schedule to the Act and Khandappa died leaving behind two sons, three daughters and a widow. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Hindu Succession Act came into force on June 17, 1956, Khandappa having died after the commencement of that Act, Khandppa 's widow would be entitled to receive a share equal to that of a son. [766C] 2. The Explanation I to section 6 of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 1929 conferred heirship rights on the son 's daughter, her share therein will be 1/6th. The proviso to section 4 makes it clear that in a partition of the coparcenary property Khandappa would have obtained a 1/4th share in his deceased husband ' s share therein and 2/7th share would devolve upon his heirs to claim on intestacy a share in their favour. [769G] 3. In view of the provisions contained in Explanation I, it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain the share of the deceased in the coparcenary properties, one cannot go back on that assumption and ascertain the shares of the heirs without reference to it. The assumption which the statute requires to be made that a partition had in fact taken place between the deceased and his coparceners immediately before his death is correct. [765H; 766A] 4. In the instant case, by application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Act, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener 's property would devolve according to the proviso, has to be determined according to terms of the testamentary instrument if any made by the deceased. [763C] 5. The fiction created by Explanation I is intended to be explanatory of the provision contained in the section, what the Explanation provides has to he correlated to the subject matter which the section itself deals with.

The respondent Corporation was established on 1st September, 1956. Under the Act the expression 'appointed day ' is de fined as the date on which the Corporation is established. The Act provided for the establishment and incorporation of the Corporation. Section 11(2) of the Act provides that every whole time employee of an insurer whose controlled business has been transferred to and vested in the Corpora tion shall retire on completion of 58 years of age but the competent authority may, if it is of opinion that it is in the interest of the corporation to do so direct such employee to retire on completing the age of 55 years. The respondent Corporation had its own establishment at New Delhi and providing for its management. On the passing of the Ordinance the management of the controlled business of all insurers was vested in India under the Act. When the Corporation came into existence it had no employees of its own to carry on the vast business of the large number of insurers which had been taken over by it. Transfer of service of existing employees of the erstwhile insurers on 31st August, 1956 was governed by the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1951. The Corporation was accordingly established on Ist September, 1957. Under section 11(1) of that Act the Central Government and the Corporation were to be established on the appointed day all the assets and liabilities appertaining to the controlledbusiness of all the insurers vested in it or for the purpose of reducing the remuneration payable to employees in cases where in the interests of the Corporatio nal business had been transferred. The appellant Corporation was therefore established on January 1, 1956 under the Life Inspec tive Act, 1948. On March 31, 1956 the Central Govern ment promulgated the Life insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956 providing for the vesting of the management in India and pending the appointment of the custodians for the controlled Business of all its insurers. The Ordinance was replaced by the (Staff) Regulations, 1960 which provided that the age Of retirement at 55 years subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement shall be 60 years as in the case of Class III and Class IV employees who entered service prior to 1st Septem ber, 1956 shall retire from the date of the appointedday. The first proviso to regulation 21 of the ( Staff) Regulations was replaced with effect from July 1, 1960 by the Amendment Act 17 of 1957 which provided for a shorter notice of termination. It was felt that clause (b) of section 49(2), as amended in 1981, had no reference to the other terms and conditions of service. Thereafter sub section (1) Of section 11 of the Life Assa ture Regulations, 1956, made it applicable to all employees who had become employ ees of the appellant Corporation under sub section(1). The first Proviso to regulation 22 of the Staff Regulations, 1957 was amended by introducing clause (bb) in sub section 2 of section 11. Sub regulation (2) was again amended on 21st January, 1977 and in directing that the Corporation shall continue the services of all employees as to their remuneration in such manner as it thought fit and if the alteration was not acceptable to any employee the Corporation might terminate his employment on giving him compensation equivalent to three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The second proviso to Regulation 21 of 1981 provided for an additional period of termination of service with such employee as would have held the same on the appointment day if the Act had not been passed, and would continue to do until and unless his employment in the Corporation was terminated and until his employment was terminated or until his remuneration in the corporation was terminated. The proviso to that sub section provided for another shorter notice period of service without assigning any reason. The third proviso to the Regulation made a distinction between an employee who entered the service of the respondent Corporation after it was established, i.e., after 1st October 1956 and the transferred employees insofar as the age o f superannuation was concerned.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to the Prime Minister, Chief Justice of India and the Prime Ministers. The letter was signed by 15 members of the Bar Association. The appellants were informed that the matter would be referred to the Chief Justice for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The Chief Justice sent a letter addressed to the Union Minister, who stated that the file could be traced to the Registrar in a closed cover. The Registrar told them that the closed cover could reach the Hon 'ble Chief Justice and left the letter with the Registrar. The Secretary of the State Government wrote to the appellants that the case could be transferred to the High Court for being placed before the Chief justice for being taken over. The High Court did not take any action against the two persons on the letter written by them. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the contents of the letter which they addressed to others and others were correct; (2) that there was no intention whatsoever on their part to scandalise the Honble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The letters written by the appellants were correct. It is not a contempt. All we need say that it will not be correct and proper for any Judge to accept the invitation and hospitality of any busi ness or commercial organisation or any club or organisation run on sectarian, communal or parochial lines. Invitations by the Bar Associations or any Club organisation or organisation running on sectary, communal, parochal lines.invitations by public discusses and criticises the views expressed by him. [247E G] 2. The Judges are by reason of their office and nature of work expected not to get involved in controversial matters, or to concern themselves with political issues or policies taken by political parties as a part of their political programme. They are by virtue of their status and nature. Not expected to get involve in controversil al matters, nor to concern itself with political issue or policies under political issues. Invitation by the bar associations or organisation or of any club organisation or association run on religious sectarian or communal parochtic lines. [245F G] 3. The Judge travels from his judicial work and descends into the arena of politics and parties. The judge cannot in such a case take shelter behind his office if the public discussers and criticise the views expressing by him.[247A B] 4. The Court does not sit much less substantial ly with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the courts. [246F G; 246B] 5. The order of the High court is utterly unsound and unsus tainable.

The petitioner was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The petitioner was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute and cloth. In connection with its business, it had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded taxa tion. On the basis of the report of the Commission appointed under section 5(1) of the Act, the Central Government referred the cases to the Investigation Commission for investigation. The Commission appointed by the Investigation Com mission included in the report the commission of the offence. The petitioners challenged the validity of the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act and the rules framed thereunder on the ground that they contravened articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as they had made good profits which they had not disclose and had thereby evaded tax. Held, that section 5 (4) of Act XXX of 1947 was not void as it gave arbitrary power to the Commission to pick and choose the cases of persons who fell within the group of those who had evaded payment of tax to a substantial extent. The procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in sections 6 and 7 was more drastic than the procedure prescribed in sections 37 and 38 of the Income tax act, 1922. The provisions of section 5 were not intended to be exhaustive but only to persons who made extraordinary profits and to a large extent evaded payment thereof. The power conferred on the Commission under section 34 of the said Act is an extra ordinary one and must be exercised by the Central Govern ment or the State Government in the first instance. The powers possessed by the Commission are not limited to those which have evaded taxation but are exercisable only with persons who had escaped assessment. The impugned Act was a valid classification and deals with a group of persons, who came within the class of war profiteers which required special treatment and that the classification is rational and reasonable grounds existed for making distinction between those who fell outside the group. The classification is reasonable and proper and it cannot be said that the discriminatory procedure adopted by the State was not in accordance with the provisions Of section 5.

The appellant Federation was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The business of the Federation carried on in the premises was a 'trade, business or profession ' within the definition of section2(5). The Association had its registered office at New Delhi. It was carrying on the business of importing Indian goods and exporting finance and all other economic subjects connected with the common good of India. The appellant Federation had its own business in Delhi. In the course of its business, it had its principal objects and sought to promote industrial development and marketing of various kinds of products. The Association was registered under section 26 of the . The objects of the Association were: (a) To promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade; (b) To secure organised action on all subjects connected With the common ' good of Indian business; (c) To ensure organised action by all subjects dealing with the Common good of the Indian business. The Society was registered as a "trade, profession or business" within section 2 (5). In its memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and other material, which was more or less the same, were referred to. The Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishment, Delhi, called upon the Federation to register its establishment under the Act, and the Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2 of the Act. The Federation then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order, dated February 4, 1964 passed by the Chief Inspector, and for a writ of Prohibition directing the Magistrate not to proceed with the complaint. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the premises of the Union were not a commercial establishment within the term of section 3(5), and that the activities carried on by the Federation were not 'a business or trade ' in general. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The definition of "commercial Establishment" is wider than that of "shop". A systematic activity can be a business activity even if no dividends are declared or shared profits. [352 D] (2) The word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a trade, how can it be denied that the Council carries on any business or industry ? [353 E F] (3) The activity of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the definition if the activity carried on was by it amounts to a busi lature. It is well settled that a systematic activity cannot be a "shops" or a " commercial establishment". It is also well settled in a systematic and organised activity that a regular activity can, therefore, bring it within the ambit of a "sshop" or "commercial establishments". [353 G H] (4) The activities of the Society are also in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'industry '. Though the rendering or service is not specifically mentioned as an element of the defined definition of commercial establishment, yet this very element appears in the definition as defined by section 2.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his descendants. During the previous year of assessment years 1949 50, the Province of Benares was ceded to British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpore and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Ausan Singh. It appears that in 1796 there were some disputes between Babu A, A, B, C, D and D which were referred by the Collector of Benaras to the Board of Revenue in Calcutta. The question was whether the pension or allowance was agricultural income for the year 1949 50. Held, that the grant of varying and unspecified amount received by the assessee as remuneration was not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of the fund was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of the pension was discovered, it was not taxable on the ground that the allowance varied from year to year. Held further, that though an annuity is not always taxable as income, it is ordinarily taxable income in his hands. The amount paid as remuneration is not in consideration of the value of the property and not its periodicity. The character of the income is, therefore, altered when a part of the Income of the Trust is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the net income of an estate for his capital sum payable in installments. The source of such pension was a contingent one and not taxable.

The appellants in Civ il Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors 'A ' in various departments in pursuance of a circular dated 6th November 1962 issued by the Director General of Ordnance Factories, Government of India, Ministry of Defen tials, New Delhi. The appellants in Civil Appeal No 441/81 were promoted to the post of Chargeman Grade II on 2 years ' satisfactory service in order to chargeman grade II. They filed writ petitions before this Court praying for a direction to the respond ents to promote them to the next higher posts of Chargemen Grade I, Assistant Foreman and Foreman, and also for a direc tions to promote the appellants to the said post from the next high er scale. The respondents in their counter affidavit contended that under the rules of promotion from Supervisor 'A" to Supervisor 'B ' there was no scope for automatic promo tion only on completion of 2 years of service as Chargeman Gr. II, and that the appellants were entitled to be promoted to these posts even if they were found unfit to be promote. The respond ent No. 1 contended that in accordance with the said rule the cases of all the appellants had been screened by the Promotion Commit tee no right would accu nate to them inasmuch as such promo tion would be in the teeth of Rule 12 and could not confer a legal right on the appel lants to be likewise promoted in breach of Rule 13. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled to get their present sala ry promotion from the date they were appointed to Chargeman grade 11 i.e. from the dates their junior was promoted. At the most they would be entitled to refixation of the salary on the basis of the notional seniority gran t ed to them in different grades so that their present pay ment is not lower than those who are immediately below them. [109E F] 1.2 The appellants have been discriminated by depriving them of automatic promotion in violation of Article 16 of the Constitution. They have been discriminat ed by depriving the benefit of automatic promo tions in violation o f Rule 12. With regard to the plea based on Articu nal principle, this court is not inclined to accept the contention that those Supervisors ' A ' who had joined much later than 20th January 1966 stood in a class separate from those whose promo tion was to be made thereafter.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the respondent in W.P. No. 4053 of 1985, granted permits to the appellant State Tourism Development Corporation and two other permits to it for the purpose of promoting tourism. The State Government issued a notification under section 63(7) of the , directing that the Karnataka State Tourism development Corporation and the two permits be granted to private operators and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpn. from one to three. The appellant State Road transport Corporation, in its proceedings dated April 30, 1984, granted 11 out of eleven permits to private operator and increased number of permit to private stage operators and increase the number. The Karnataka State Transport Corporation set aside the grant of two permits in favour of the appellant, which was challenged by some of the private operators on the ground that the preference contemplated by the proviso to section 63 (7) contemplated exclusion of the 'non preferred category ' if sufficient number of applicants from the classes were available. The Tribunal held that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the Proviso to section 64(7), the preference became operative only if other things were equal. It also held that the appellant had not been denied the grant on the grounds that the ' non preferred category had to be excluded as the number was of permits to be granted. The High Court, however, allowed the writ petitions and set aside its order dated February 28, 1985 setting aside the 'succession ' in favour the Karnataka state Road Transport Corpora tion and instead granted three out of nine permits to public stage operators. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the grant Of two permits to a State Road Trans port Corporation was set aside because the State Transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter State Transport Undertakings would have priority; and (ii) the appellant 's expertise and resources were better equipped to render the same. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme excludes omnibus operators and requires applicants to have two years experience in the car hire business or that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies of either indigenous make or acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the vehicle hire business. [1016C D] 2. The terms and conditions to be fulfilled are that are: (i ) the party must have been in the ' car hire ' business for a period of 2 years with the help of cars of indigenous cars or make indigenous cars obtained from elsewhere and should have sufficient contacts with travel agencies hoteliers/apartments, etc. and should be financially sound or that he should be owned and financially sound; (ii ) the application of the Undertaking shall be given preference over other applicants. [106E F] 3. The Scheme makes no reference to the proviso in section 63 of the . On the other hand it mentions that the rules of preference will apply only if the other conditions are equal. [1006F G] 4. The policy underlying the proviso is to be given priority over other applications. While it is true that section 47(1 H) does not expressly refer to "other things being equal", it appears to be implicit in the provision that other things are equal, and the application Of the Undertaking will have preference over others. [ 1016C] 5.

The respondent purchased by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju. The respondent claimed that he was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of sales tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The Commercial Tax Officer and the Board of Revenue, who tried the case, held that Rule 21 A was ultra vires the power of the State Government under sections 19(1) and (2) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. The High Court in appeal reversed the judgment of the single Judge holding that r. 21 A did not apply to the respondent 's case as he had no authority under section 19(2)(c) of Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of thebusiness was made liable for the arrears. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Rule 21A is beyond the rule making power of State Government either under section19(1), or section 19 (2)(C) of Madras General Clauses Act (Madras Act No. 1 of 1891). The liability to tax does not depend upon assessment. The liability is definitely created by sections 3 and 4 of the Income Tax Act which are charging sections and the assessment order under section 23 only quantifies the liability which has already been definitely and finally created by the charging sections. [663 B C] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; , applied.

The appellant, who was a Government servant, was dismissed from service on account of certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The appellant filed a suit against the State of Bombay for a declaration that the order of dismissal passed by the lower appellate court was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution as according to him, there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer and that the appellant had not asked for copy of it. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : The decree of the High court decreeing payment of arrears of salary is truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of tile Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. [922 C] The decree was passed on the basis of arrears and not on merits. It was not necessary for the Government servant to have asked for a copy. [936 G H] In reilly vs R. ; , referred to. (1) The High Court had decreed payment of salary in proceedings under section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation, Act, as according by that rule no duty could be imposed on a Government Servant for arrears of pay because he was not actually in office. [940 G H; 923 A] (2)(i) The words "actionable wrong other than breach of contract" in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servants for arrears salary of salary the decree properly falls under section 61. [945 C D] (ii) The decree passed by both the lower courts was not liable to be set aside on the grounds that it had no application to the case of arrears. The High court had therefore rightly held that the decree of Rs. 2,690 being a liability arising out of a contract, the decree should properly fall under section 63 of the Act rather than under section 62. [946 E F] (iii) In view of the decision in State of Tripura vs The Province of East Bengal ; , it is not necessary to decide whether reasonable opportunity has been afforded to the Government servants to have called for a report from the Enquiry officer.

The appellant and the respondent were adjoining colliery owners. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of certain coal from the appellant 's land. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondents had encroached upon the appellant coal, that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below was vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. Held: (i) The High Court had rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had knowledge of the encroachment only within three years of the date of filing of the suit. (ii) The respondents had knowledge that the appellant had encroached on the land in question and was thus wholly unworkable, entirely lost to them for ever. In the written statement they did not deny the fact that the coal still left in the encroached area was not by any means available to them. (iii) The finding of the High court that the appellants had knowledge was based on mere probabilities without clear evidence to sustain them. Held further, that there is no presumption under section 101 of the Indian Contract Act that the burden in the former sense is upon the party who comes to Court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. That burden is constant throughout the trial; but the burden to prove in the sense of adducing evidence shifts from time to time having regard to the evidence adduced by one party or the presumption of fact raised in favour of one or the other. In such cases the burden is upon a party who brings to Court the existence Of certain facts and which he asserted. That onus is constant during the trial, but the onus to prove that he obtained the knowledge of his father was within three year of the alleged trespass. The burden of proving that he had knowledge must be on the respondents. But the question is whether they have adduced evidence which had the effect of shifting the onus of proof to establish the fact of encroachment only in 1941. Held, further, (i)(a) that the High Courts were right in accepting the boundaries drawn from the plan drawn up by the Court tested the position of the six trijunction pillars shown in the map of lease dated November 23, 1900, and found that two of the trijugal pillars were in their correct positions. The courts below had held that these plots were mostly outside the encroached areas and that the quarries were mostly within the encroached portion, there were only underground workings and that they were mostly inside the encroached land. (b)that the respondents could not claim exemption from the operation of rule 76 of the Mineral Mines Regulation, 1946, as it was not permissible to ignore the starting point of the boundary line and adopt any scientific point based on survey. Held also, further that the evidence in the present case did not prove that the structures were mostly beyond the encroached limit. The High court had rightly found that the defendants had knowledge about the encroachment of their coal mines only in the year 1941 which was within 3 years of their date of the filing of suit.

The appellant was a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It was alleged that on June 21, 1958, the Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21,, 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Industrial Court had jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. In the present case the employer could defend the action under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders which is a term of contract between the appellant and its employees to dispense with the service of any employee at any time by giving 14 days notice or paying 12 days wages. The Industrial Court in appeal had jurisdiction under r, 18(a) to interfere and set it aside such an order. The employer could not defend the proceedings under r., 18 (b). The Industrial Tribunal had no power under that rule to interfere with the order of discharge passed by the appellant. The power given by r.18 (a), of the standing orders in this case, was subject to the scrutiny of industrial courts in the manner indicated above. The appellant could not rest its case merely on r. 19 (a). Held further, that under the contract he had unfettered right "to hire and fire" his employees. That right is now subject to industrial adjudication and even a power like that granted by r.,18 (b) of tho Standing Orders in this ease, is subject to scrutiny of Industrial courts in this manner indicated in the present appeal.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for declaration of their rights to exhibit motion pictures and entertainment performances etc. The trial court passed an order rejecting the objection on the ground that the document dated November 27, 1954 was not a lease. The High Court dismissed the revision application holding that the documents were not of law and that the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease or other character had to be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent , it must be held that in view of the consent order of December 1, 1960, the respondents were debarred from leading any evidence of the plaintiffs in view Of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The appellant contended that an enquiry into the nature or legal relationship arising out of the agreement dated December 1.1960 was barred by the principle of res judicata and estoppel under the provisions of section 92. The Trial Court rejected the contention and held that the evidence as to the true nature of the transaction was not inadmissible by virtue of section 91 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The respondents appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The consent decree must be treated as res judicata because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the par ties to a suit which is superadded the seal of the Court. A consent decree does not operate as resjudicata merely because a decision on any issue of the issues is in fact a judgment in rem. [437 C] (ii) The order passed by the High Court was set aside and the Trial Court directed to proceed and dispose of the suit.

The respondent was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms and conditions contained in the said order includ ing the above term relating to the above terms relating to his period of appointment and on his accepting the terms, conditions contained therein. The services of the respondent were extended retrospectively from 1st August, 1985 by an order dated 20th August, 1979. The re spondent was required by the Government to furnish the acceptance of his terms and condi tions contained in that order including the above mentioned term relating tot he above said term relating t he period of his appointment which extended only upto 30th August 1985. The High Court allowed the Review Petition filed by the respondent relying on an interim order dated 10.7.1986 passed by the Governor. In support of the review petition, the respondent relied on an order passed by a Single Judge in which it was provided that one post will be kept vacant and in case the petitioner succeeds in his petition it would be made available forthwith to the petitioner by way of an appointment. The petitioner challenged the said interim order before this Court contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. Allowing the Review Peti tion, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent had not urged before the High Court that the order of appointment issued in his case was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period to the post till 30th of August 1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. Even the order passed on review is wholly unsustainable. [245E F] 1.2 The respondent, who was not satisfied by the interim order, had put forward at that stage such a case. His only case was that the interim ord er conferred on him a right to continue in service beyond 30th September 1985, even though his service had not been extended by the Govern ment nor of Uttar pradesh. [246F G] 1:3 The respondent could not be treated to have the effect of controlling the jurisdiction of the High Courts to dispose of the Writ Petition on merits as it did on 24.3.1988. He should have preferred an appeal before this court and that was done on 24th March, 1988. [243G H] 1(a) The order passed in review is unsustainable. It is open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the petitioner for a continution service in a post or the fresh appointment and no observations in this regard are being made by this Court.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had no motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 's case is covered by section 302 I.P.C. [368E] 2. It flows out of the fundamental principle of our criminal jurisprudence that the accused is entitled to the benefit of any reasonable doubt. If two reasonably probable and evenly balanced views of the evidence are possible, one must necessarily concede the existence of a reasonable doubt and fanciful possibilities must be left out of account. To entitle an accused person to the benefits of a doubt arising from the possibility of a duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly probable as that against him. If the preponderance of probability is all one way, a bare possibility of another view will not entitle the accused to claim the benefit Of any doubt. [369B C] 3. The principle that "if two reasonable conclusions can be reached on the basis of the evi dence which is barely possible, it is the obvious duty of the High Courts to interfere in the interest of justice lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule. That is what the High court has done in this case. [370C D] 4. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. The order of the Trial Court should not disturb the finding of the trial court.

The appellant, a public servant, was charged with criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case against him was that he had demanded and accepted illegal gratification from his master and servant for which he had no authority to remove him from office. He was prosecuted for having committed an offence of criminal misconduct as defined in section 2(5) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act,1947. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the Judge of the Supreme Court as well as the High Court were not within the purview of the Act and that he could be tried under section 6(1) (c) of that Act only if he had in his possession pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income. The High Court held that the appellant was a public servants within the meaning of section 2 (5) and that the President had not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the High Courts or of the Privy Council from his office, though the Presi dent appointed the Judge by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The appellant contended that he was entitled to be tried for having contravened section 5 (1) of Act, because the Judge had not given the exclusive powers or the sole authority to the Chairman to remove the Judge from office within the contemplation of section 6 (1)(c). The respondent contended that the Judges of the Division Bench were not 'other than the Chief justice of the Madras High Court and that they could be prosecuted for criminal misconduct only under section 161(2) of Indian Penal Code, 1860. The question was whether a Judge of a High Court or a Judge thereof is a public officer within the definition of section 3 (1), Prevention ofcorrup tion) Act, i.e., an 'public servant ' within the ambit of that expression in sub section (1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code and the Rules framed thereunder are strong reasons to hold that for the purpose of clause (c), the Judge must be a public Servant. He falls within the sweep of the definition provided under the second requirement under clause (e) in sub s.(1). [217B C] 2. The expression 'public servants ' in section 5 of the 1947 Act means a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his place save by or with the sanction of the Central Government, of the State Government. [218D E] 3. The scheme envisaged for appointment of the superior Judges would ensure that by an honest exercise performed by all constitutional functionaries of their obligation in the process of appointment of a superior Judge, there would be no occasion to try and punish any appointee to such a high office for an act of corruption.

The appellant was a Sunri caste. He challenged the election of the respondent to a seat in the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad constituency on various grounds. The Tribunal held that the respondent 's case was that he belonged to the Saha group within the Sunri Caste and not a member of any Schedule Caste. On appeal by the Election Tribunal, the High Court set aside the decision of the Tribunal and directed the election to be set aside on the ground that the appellant bore the surname Saha and was thereby excluded from the Scheduled Castes specified in item 40 though he was a ' Sunri ' by caste but was excluded from Schedule Caste specified in Item 40. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal had gone wrong in considering the Sahas as an independent caste. [391 D] (ii) The respondent called witnesses to establish that the appel lant belonged to a smaller group of Sahas. He must be held to belong to the Scheduled Caste specified under item 40. That being so, the election petition must fail. [392 E F] (iii) The order of the Election Tribu nal dismissing the petition must be set at naught on the view that the Tribunal had not gone wrong. [390 B C] (iv) The appeal must necessarily be dismissed. [394 D] In the instant case, the evidence led in a case may be imperfect. Suppose the evidence in another case led to the conclusion, as it might conceivably do, that there was a smaller caste within the ' Sunari caste. It is legitimate to think that if the excluded Sahas were those Sunri castes, a smaller groups of Saha s, they would then have read "Sunri" excluding those who bore the prename Saha. [393 E] (v) The finding that Sahas constituted a distinct class wholly outside the Sunari Caste was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue. Evidence cannot alter the natural interpretation of the words in the Order.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215. It was arranged that the complainant should bring with him Rs. 1,000 for the articles of furniture (Exhibit E) a letter to the Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Committee for transfer of the telephone connection to the name of the complainant. The appellant and his wife were leaving the flat, the man who masked as the complain ant 's brother threw off his disguise and disclosed his identity. The police party, who was down below ready for the raid, held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers that were handed over to him by the appellant. As the appellant was not in possession of the flat he filed a complaint against the complainant under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The Presidency Magistrate acquitted the appellant but it was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. On appeal to the High Court it was contended that the word "relinquishment" in section 19(1)(a) of Act did not mean "relul tation within the meaning of that expression and was used in the Transfer of Property Act only for the purpose of making necessary ar rangements about his interest and possession under the lease. Held, that the words "the relinquishment of tenancy of any premises" in the section must be strictly construed in favour of the subject. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the case of relinquishment it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour o the lessor by mutual agreement between them. The relin cation of possession must be to the lessor or one who holds his interest. In fact, a surrender or relinquishment terminates the lessee 's rights and lets in the lessor. It is no doubt true that the term "relivish ment" does not occur in the transfer of property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour Of the landlord by notice given to him in writing.

The appellant company served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal referred to various considerations which prevailed with it in giving retrospectivity to the revised pay scales and other reliefs awarded. In its award dated December 20, 1978 the Industrial Tribu nal held that the existing wage scale was fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The appellant company filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance. The Industrial Tribun nal rejected the demand of the union and held that in view of the revised basic wages there would be a resultant increase in the dearness allowance and house rent allowance, and that the dearness allowances granted by the appellant made little impact in neutralising the cost of living. The need for revising the wage scale had been felt to give rise to an increased wage bill, and the prevailing wage structure on an industry cum region basis. Wage scale statements were filed before the Industrial tribunal which was numbered I T. No. 292 of 1975. The Union filed a Statement before the Tribu lal in July 1974 claiming an increase in dearness allowance, but that statement was accepted by the Tribunal. In proceedings to revise the wage structure and dearness allowances the Tribunal held that it was unable to rely on them as comparable concerns. Holding it impossible in the circumstances to apply the principle of industry cum Region basis, the Tribunal turned to a consideration of the financial capacity of the company to bear an additional burden. The appeal filed by the workmen was dismissed by the Industrial Appellate Tribunal.

The appellant, a sugar factory, was awarded wages for the period of one year and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. The appellant paid its employees only as their employees. As the payment of their salaries did not fall within the definition of wages under section 2(vi) of the Act, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the Patna High Court challenging the correctness of the conclusion of the authority that the applications made by the res pondents were competent under section 15 Of the Act. The High Court held that section 15 was applicable to the case because the wages prescribed by it did amount to wages as defined by section 2 (vi) and that the application made by them were incompetent under section 16 Of the , and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Under the unamended definition of "wages", it is essential to bear in mind the scope and character of the powers conferred on Industrial Tribunals when they deal with industrial disputes under the provisions of the Indus trial Disputes Act. It is now well settled that unlike ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms of contract between the parties when they dealt with disputes arising between them in respect of the said terms, Industrial adjudication is not bound to uphold the terms Of the contract between them and the employees. If it is shown to the satisfaction of industrial adjudication that the terms thereof of contract of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable. [422 C D] (ii) The true legal position in the matter is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed by the award cannot be treated as wages under s 2(v) of Act before it was amended.

The appellant was charged with criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51 and after a full trial, he acquitted him. The High Court held that the prosecution had not established that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parma and that the Chief Secretary had committed a mistake in sending the communication to convey sanction of the Government to his prosecution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the appel lant was illegal as sanction required under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure could not be obtained for prosecuting him under section 409, because, (i) the charge against the appellant was under section 411 and no sanction was required for a prosecution under that section; (ii) the prosecution which had resulted in the conviction was initiated without any sanction under section 196(1), Cr. P.C., before the appellant could be prosecuted under section 420, I.P.C. HELD: The High court was right in holding that sanction under s. 197(i) of Criminal Proce dure Code was necessary for prosecuting the appell lant under section409, and the absence of such sanction was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. [1308 G] (a) The appellant received the sum of Rs 51 alleged to have been misappropriated as Sub division Officer, and he admitted receipt of the same. Then it was his duty to pay that amount to Parma, and take his signature or thumb impression in acknowledgment thereof. The accused did not claim to have spent the amount in the course of his official duties but stated that the moneys had been con sumed by fire. It was no part of the duty of the accused to remove medicines to his house, and could not arise at the stage of sanction which mu_t precede the institution of the Prosecution. [1408 H; 1409 A B] (b) The sanction under S. 197 (1) Cr.P.,C. was required under s, 197(2), Cr P. C., before a person could be charged with it. The acts complained of were so integrally connected with the duties attached to his care as a public servant. If what appears on the face of the roll is true and whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stages of sanction then the acts with which the appellant is charged fall within the scope of his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. Clearly, therefore, sanction was necessary under section 198(1). [1309 H; 1310 A B]. (c) The prosecution which has resulted in conviction of a public officer on a charge of criminal misappropriation will depend on whether the acts complained off hinge on his duties as a pubic servant. if they are unconnected with such duties then sanction under sec. 197 is necessary. But if they were unconnected with the duty, then sanction is necessary; but if they arc unconnected with some duties then no sanction is required. [1209 G H] (d) The offence of criminal misapplying money entrusted to his own care as public servant, acts done by him in the discharge of his duty and can he justified by virtue as done under his office, because that would really be a matter of defence on the merits which would have to be in vestigated at the trial.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in Travancore State. It filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90,947 representing only the profit made by it in Travancore and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Income tax Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 as loss from branches situate outside the State. The Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. On appeal by the Commissioner of Income tax, the High Court held that a banking business could be set off against the profit of Rs, 38,998 arising in Travancore state. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i). The first proviso to section 24(1)(a) of Travancore Income Tax Act is not only affected the generality of the main enactment but also introduced an addition thereto. It carves out an exception to the main provision to which it has been enacted as a proviso and to no other. [269 G] (ii) The expression "any Indian State" in the proviso to sub section (1) of section 24 means business in British India. That would be straining the language of section 10 and would necessitate addition of words in section 10 which are not there in the section. It has to operate in the same field and if the language is clear it cannot be used for the purposes of interpreting the main provisions or to exclude something which otherwise would have been within the section, [269 A] (iii) The proviso to the second proviso to s. 24(i)(a), does not circumscribe the proviso, to business alone, but excludes something which would otherwise have been in the Act. It is a fundamental rule of construction that a proviso must be considered with relation to the principal matter to which the it stands as proviso. [270 B] (iv) The words "any India" are used in a proviso to a particular provision of a statute only embraces the field which is covered by the main section i.e., section 24 (1). Therefore, the mere use of the words " any Indian State ' in the second schedule to section 10 would necessitate add of words therein cannot be construed as enlarging the scope of an enactment when it can be fairly and properly construed without attributing to it that effect.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co. was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of Shaw Wallace and Co., which had been ,doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947 the Private Limited company was converted into a Public Limited Company with effect from August 1959. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The Company resisted the workmen 's claim but contended that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees similar provisions similar to those which had already been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees, and that in any particular region employees had been successful in their claim for fixing the age at 60 years, and therefore, the Tribunal should not disturb the award fixing the retirement age of the workmen. The Tribunal rejected the Company 's contention and held that it would be appropriate to introduce a change in the age for its employees in all industries in Bombay region. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem was not very commendable and that its present conclusion was not quite commendable. The approach adopted was not too commendable, and it had ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. In spite of these infirmities, the award of the Tribunal directed that the age should be fixed at 60. Accordingly, the norm for retirement age was fixed at 58.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1961 and had an authorised capital of Rs. 1 crore divided into 1,00,000 shares of Rs 100 each. Its primary object was to carry on business of manufacturing all types of barium compounds. The Company Law Board made an order under section 237(b) of the , appointing 4 persons as Inspectors for investigating the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. 2 as Inspectors and appointed 3 to 6 as Inspectors. On June 4, 1965 the company sent a notice to M/s Mitchell Ltd. stating that if the plant was not completely installed and got into running order by June 1, 1965, the Company will have to make alternative arrangements and that it would hold M/S. T. The firm of T. T., the appellant No 2 as Inspector for investigating its affairs of Barium Chemical Ltd. The company Law Board sent a letter to M /s Mithell Ltd., on April 2, 1965 in which the Company stated that if it was not fully installed and get into running orders by June l, 1965 it will have made alternative arrangements. On April 2. 1965 the Company sent a reply to M 's Mitavell Ltd . stating that the plant had been completely installed, got into run order by May 1,1965 and approved by the Central Government in November of that year. Thereafter a permit for importing the requisite machinery was granted to the company. The appellant No 1 issued a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the order of May 19, 1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the order having been made at the instance of the shareholders is invalid and on a true construction of section 237 (b) it is within the discretion of the High court whether to allow a person who has sworn an affidavit before it as required by section 237. The appellants were tried and convicted for the offence of dacoity. The trial court acquitted them but the High Court, in appeal, took the view that the presumption under section 41 1.P.C., was not applicable to the case as it was raised at night by 20 persons or more. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The conviction was correct and must be set aside. The sentence of fine is reduced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment. [723 B] (ii) The offence was committed at night as many as 20 persons were the dacoits. It may be 723 noticed that from each person a large number of goods of the same type such as 20 choli pieces or ten pieces of cloth were found. It is impossible to think that within the short time available these goods could have been easily disposed of receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [823 G H] (iii) The presumption under s.41 1. P.C. was not attracted to the present case because the persons with whom the goods were found were the appellants themselves. This presumption has been drawn and in our opinion rightly in this case. [789 A B] In what circumstances the one of the presumption or the other may be drawn under section 114 of the Evidence Act, it is not necessary to state categorically in this ease that the persons who with whom they were found are the dacoits themselves. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed.

The petitioners are manufacturers of 'thinner ' containing spirit and other soluble material. They have challenged the vires of the provisions of the Indian Penal Code on the ground that the section gives an unguided, unchanelised and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the specified poison. The petitioners contended that the impugned section gave an unguided power, ununchanel ed and arbitrary powers to the state Government to exclude any substance from the poison for t he purpose of restrictions to be placed on the possesseda tion for sale of such poison. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 2 or 5 are not hit by any consti tutional limitation. [225G] 2.1 The provisions in the Indian penal Code do not confer arbitrary and uncontrolled power on the State to include a substance as medicine for the pur pose of restriction. It is a busi ness which can regulate trade. This posi tion is well settled and it would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [226A B] 2:2. The impugned section gives arbitrary, unconchan ed and uncontrolled powers to State Government in Rule 13(1) to regulate the possi sion of any specified poison in any local area in which the use of such medicine for t hat purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possession thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. [227D] 2 :3. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same. It was a bus i ness, which could be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and safety of society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the Act itself. [228E F] 2(a) The provisions are not violative of any consid eral limitation or offends the petition ers ' right to trade on any trade or business. The character of trade is such, that nobody could be considered t he have an exclusive right to deal with it. It would be inappropriate to cite the authorities in this regard. [229D] (b) The Act and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as a poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu sion the late possession and sale in that Area. No question of discrimination can arise in such circumstances. [230E F; 227A] (c) The object of the enactment is to regulate trade, which can be termed as inherently un dangerous to life. It has become a weapon of crime.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was brought into force on September 20, 1984. On September 11, 1985, the petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984, and obtained an order of stay of dispossession therein. The respondents filed a writ petition challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards were not made within two years of the making of the declaration under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the award was not made in accordance with the time limit prescribed by section 11 A of the Act and that the petitioners had a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so, his application is liable to be rejected. [567B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the stay orders were highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. The interim orders have a direct impact on the questions raised and non disclosure thereof amounts to concealment of material fact. If the petitioners fail to do this, their application is required to be dismissed. [568C] 2:2. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there was no reference in the Special leave Petitions to any to the stay order and they came to know about these orders only when the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit. In view of the provisions contained in Section 11 A(1) of the land Acquisition Act read with section 11A of the 1894 Act, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed.

The second group consisted Of workmen who entered service before January 1. 1959 and those who entered services on or after January 1,. 1959. (iv) which provided for actual calculations starts with the words "subject to rules (i) to (iii)" and therefore the actual calculations made under cl. The Tribunal held that basic pay was to be fixed as on January 31, 1959. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the adjustment of basic pay in cl. 2(d) could not be permitted in view of cl. 3(iv). The payment of the adjusted basic pay had to be made as on 1st January 1959 and therefore it was not necessary for the Bank to give effect to this clause. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee did not validly assign Rs.1,00,000 in favour of his sons or grand sons and hence the amounts had been wrongly included in his net wealth by the Income Tax officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no valid gifts. This question has been examined by various High Courts. It is possible in certain circumstances for a donor to make a valid gifts by debiting his account and crediting the account in the name of the donee. Thereafter, a host of writ petitions were filed in this Court challenging the constitutional validity of clause 'fourthly ' clauses ' and 'thirdly ' and fourthly ' of section 15(1)(b) and (c) of the Punjab pre emption. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The right of preemption conferred on a tenant is an absolute restriction on the right to hold, acquire and dispose of property under Article 19(1) (f).
