The second respondent, a son of the first wife, had executed two wills in favour of one of his sons and the same was filed in this Court. The terms of the compromise stipulated payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the father to each of them under two different wills. In February 1985, during the pendency of the special leave petition, the adoptive mother died. The alienees had also executed a will in favour one of the sons and a third respondent was also made a party. The second respondent filed an application for setting aside the compromise decree on the ground that the said alienations were valid and binding. This Court granted time to the alienees to vacate the property. In view of the fact that there had been improvements of the property by the alienee, the High Court directed that mesne profits be set off against the same. The parties have filed this appeal after obtaining special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The sale deeds are subsequent to 21.8.1987. There were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence. [541A] 1.2. In a suit for title and injunction, the alienors have no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In the instant case, the transfers are pendente lite. [543B C] 2.1 The alienee has not received the sum of Rs 1 lakh from the alieners before registering authority. The transfer of the different sale deeds would be entitled to withdraw the amounts on the basis of the record made by the Sub Registrar on each of the sale deeds and the alienorees will have no liability to account.

The workmen of the appellant company, who were employed in the manufacture of electrically electrically treated as industrial workers, claimed that they should be entitled to receive the benefit of sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. The Industrial Tribunal held that the sickness benefit would not accrue for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness which was last paid and that the workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for the second two days also. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the benefit should be given only to those who were entitled to sick leave and that they would not be entitled for any sickness benefit during the first three days of their illness. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal could not be said to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were re ceiving under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the Act. [864G] 2. The Scheme of the benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said tO mean that the workers would get benefit of the sick leave in a manner set out in the award. Such a leave could not he categorised as privilege leave, as by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the ease of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It would thus appear that the appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question are illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [874C D] 3. The benefit of a sick leave has been allowed to the workmen of those companies. It is not necessary that in the circumstances of the case to award the benefit under the sick Leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975, in the present case, the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the , became available to the employees. [884D E] 4. The appellants have filed a statement (exhibit 7) containing information regarding the companies which had provided the benefit to sick Leave to its workmen in the region. It shows that even though the Act was applicable to the workers of the Precision Bearings India Ltd., Baroda, the benefits under the scheme of the were not similar to those admissible under section 49 of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme. [854E F] 5. The appellant companies have filed their statement (Exhibit 7), containing information about the companies who had provided sick leave to its employees in the area concerned on December 14, 1969. That was obviously under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefits which the Act allowed for, as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. [834E G] 6. The workers ' State insurance Scheme does not cover all contingencies of sickness and in any event the first one waiting days are not covered. In the case, however, it is not proper for the Tribunal to have granted the benefit on full remuneration during the periods of theworkman 's physically incapacity to earning his normal wage because of sickness. It has to be appreciated that a workman is prevented from earning the normal daily wages during the second one days of his illness and there is no justification for the argument that the rate of benefit at about half his wage under the first proviso to section 49 should be considered sufficient so as to deny him the bene fit of sick Leave on full pay. [844C E] 7.

The appellant was detained under section 3 of the , as he had a standing of about thirty years. He was taken into custody and interrogated, physically assaulted and threatened with dire consequences. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of detention. The appellant challenged his detention before the High Court in a writ petition. The High Court held that the grounds furnished by the appellant were vague and that the detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan Action Committee, and that it was not necessary to mention particulars of the activities carried on by him or the details of financial aid alleged to have been received by him from the Portuguese authorities. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The order of the High court was bad because the grounds supplied were vague as they did not disclose any particulars of activities which related to the decision of the detaining author ity. [387 D] (ii) The failure to supply particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest, are vested in the detaining au thority. It follows that the authority is under a constitutional obligation to furnish particulars and to consider if the grounds which are furnished are vague or not, the satisfaction of the authori ty must be clearly communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds are furnished. [388 E] (iii) The authority is not under a Constitutional obligation to supply details in a case where no particulars are at all furnished. It is not possible to state affirmatively more on the question of what is vague. It must vary according to the circumstances of each case. If on reading the ground furnished it is capable of being understood or defined with sufficient certainty it can be called vague. [389 A B] (iv) The detaining authority is in a constitutional duty to furnish reasonably definite grounds, as well as adequate particulars and then there may or shortly thereafter. But the right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) which implies, the right to be supplied adequate particulars of grounds of detained, to enable a proper representation being made. These rights involve corresponding obligations on the part of the authority.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Training Centre, Secundrabad. He was dismissed from service on April 9, 1959. The Central Government directed removal of his service from service. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of dismissal from service and for quashing that order. The High Court held that r. 14 of the Army Rules 1954, was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that r, 14 of ' the Army Rule, 1954, which was intra vires the ; was ultra rites. HELD: The High court was right in holding that r 14 of Rules 1954 was not ultra vires. [449 B] The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 make it subject to section 45, and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words " subject to the . provisions of the Act", it speaks of removal of a person against the service. [451 E] The power under s.19 is an alternative power. Though section 19, uses the word "subject" in section 20, it speaks only of removal from service under section 16 of the read with r.14 of the Rules. Although the section uses the expression "subjects to the pro visions of this , it speaks that there should be rules and subject to provisions of Act and such rules, the Central Govern ment may dismiss or remove the officer with or without pension or gratuity if any admissible to him. Under the aforesaid r. the Central Govt. may remove a member from the Service in derogation Of section 46 of the .

The appellant company imported certain goods from the Panchayat limits of the jurisdiction of the Panchayat under r. 21 of the Rules framed by the State Government. The Panchayat was to levy octroi duty on the goods coming into its local limits, and the rates were fixed on January 14, 1964. On March 17, 1963, the State Legislature passed a resolution No. 5 authorising the imposition of octroi duty. The appellant challenged the said resolution before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that r. 5 was intra vires the powers of the rule making authority and that the Standing Committee had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits as the appeal to the Panchayat Samiti was barred by limitation because r.5 of the Fees Rules was ultra vires the power of the State. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was wrong in holding that r 5 was ultra rites the powers conferred on the State by r. 3(b). It only dealt with two items; (i) selection of tax and the rate at which it is levied. Under r.3(d), what the Panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions and then finally make the choice as regards two things i.e., the tax or fee imposed and the manner in which it was levied. Rule 3(c) has to be read alongwith r.21, and if so read, it would mean that before the octroi duty can start being levied, r.22 must be complied with. [222 B C] (2) The rule which authorises the levy is r. 22, but it enjoins that the procedure prescribed in rr.3 and 4 should be followed before the tax can start be levied from the date specified in the notice. But r.4 has to he read alongwith Rule 21, and, if so, read, the scheme of the fees Rules would mean the action taken under the Act and the rules is required to be notified to the public.

The appellants were the Andheri Marol Kurla Bus Service and were charged with having committed an offence under section 33 read with section 33 of the , for committing a breach of the provisions of section 33(1) of the . The Magistrate acquitted all the accused including the appellants but on appeal by special leave, Held, that the conciliation proceedings should be held to terminate when the Conciliation Officer is required under section 12(6) of Act and submit his report to the appropriate Government. No doubt section 12 contemplates that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings are not closed but are carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation officer does not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach Of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of that Act. The conciliation proceedings could be said to be pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed and the appellants were rightly convicted under section 31(1). Held, further, that section 12 (6) Of the , does not apply to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer are deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the report of the Conciliation Offi cer is received by the appropriate Govern ment. The provisions of sub section 2 apply to any conciliation proceeding whether in respect of utility services and otherwise.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the ground that he had been illegally and useless and that there was indiscriminate firing by him and his associates. He was also charged with offences u/s 147, 341, 353, 307/34 IPC and 27 Arms Act. In the case of the petitioner, the detaining authority stated that the activities of the detenu 's brother and the petitioner have disturbed the normal tempo of life in Katras and Jogta Police Stations in Dhanbad area. The grounds of detention were served on him at about 2 p.m. on 24th December 1985. He challenged his detention before the High Court which was dismissed without any speaking order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated by the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of Preventive detention should not be exercised. In this case, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there were such a possibility of release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authori ties properly and seriously before the service of the order. A bald statement is merely an ipso dixit of the officer. If there are cogent materials for thinking that the detenu might he be released then these should have been made apparent. [910C D] 2. The detention order was passed on the basis of the said principles. There was rational nexus between the object of the detention and the circumstances alleged. In these circumstances, it appears that before the services there was consideration of all the relevant factors, the petitioner could not have been put into preventive custody.

The appellant company was a dealer in gold. The respondent, who carried on business as a money lender or banker, filed a petition under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 for the issue of a writ of prohibition against the appellant company from carrying on any business in gold and ornaments. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the ground that it suffered from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been laid nor any particular guide line has been expressly indicated in section 28 by reference to which the Administrator is required to exercise his power. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Courts were not right in holding that section 28 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. [954F] Harakchand Banthias vs Asstt. Collector of Central Excise, Poona Division II, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamdas Chokshi vs Union of India & Ors., , relied on. The restrictions imposed by section 28 are meant to prevent the circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Therefore, in the absence of any parity of situation or the doctrine of parity of reasoning cannot be invoked. [936A] Harkchand Banthia 's case, ; referred to. In the instant case, the restrictions which have been imposed in section28 are meant for preventing the circum stances of other provision of the , and by the prime consideration that circumvention thereof shall not be premitted. Having regard to this position which obtains in the case section 28 cannot be struck down on the grounds of excessive delegated delegation of power. [940C] Harakhchand Banthuas vs Asst.

The appellants filed a suit for declaration of their title to the properties in question and for possession. The trial Judge held that the grant of the Inam was a personal Inam, and that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of section 87 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (No. XIX of 1951), and that the appellants were entitled to the possession of the properties. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court had rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of a temple but in their individual character as owners of the said properties. The mere fact that the parties were in management of the temple did not show that they had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of the temples. The High Court was right in holding that the title of the Temple had not been lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed. Held, further, that there is no evidence on record to show, that any alienor had been appointed by another person who was in management, of the suit temple as de jure trustees of the appellant 's family and that they were not holding the same as managers of it. The fact that a alienor was still alive did not mean that the transferor or disposed of all the property and left the village with all its properties. In fact, the alienor could not be said to have resigned his office or left it.

The appellant, a partnership firm consisting of himself and the two persons aforementioned, was running a modern cinema complex on hire in Collaboration with two osher persons. The said firm applied to the District Magistrate under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 for permission to construct a modern Cinema Hall at the proposed site, a detailed description of which was furnished in the plan annexed to the application. The District Magistrate rejected the request of the appellant and declared Shri Ved Gupta as the sole licensee. On appeal by the respondents, the District Judge set aside the order passed by the District Magis trate and held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Sharma, who had been declared to be the sole licensees in respect of the Apsara Theatre. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by him. The learned Single Judge allowed the appeal holding that the District magistrate had no power under section 6 F of the Act or the Rules to suspend a licence pending the proceed ings for such revocation, the district Magistrate had no jurisdiction or power to suspend the licence pending proceedings for such revoking, the license and that the only power vested in the licensing authority was to revoke the licence under section 4 F of Act. The Division Bench held that where the licensed premises including the cinematographs used therein belonged to a partnership and one of the partners had obtained a licence in his separate name, the other partners automatically acquired an interest in the licence. On the question whether the license in respect Of the Apara Theatre was granted by the district magistrate in favour of the respondent, the Division Bench took the view that where a licensed premises include the cinematograph,s used in the premises and hence it necessarily follows that where such licensed premises includes the cinematograph used therein belong to a firm and one or of the partner had obtained an order in his own name, he alone acquired an interests in the license. The High Court held that since the licensing authorities had no authority under the Act before the licence was suspended, the impugned order was void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the district Magis trrate had no powers or power under the Rules and that only the power vested by the licensing authori ties was to cancel the licence granted in favour the respondent; (ii) that even though the licence had originally been issued in the names of the cinema business, the right of operation of the license had become the property of the theatre by virtue of clauses 13 and 18 of the partnership deed and since Ved Gupta had been expelled from the partnership and had thereby ceased to be connected with the firm, he did not have the possession of the premises; (iii) that in any event, the licensing au thority was right in holding that there was no legal right in the licensee which entitled it to notice and hearing under the Jammu & Kashmir (Control of Building and Maintenance) Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order is one passed by a District Magistrate in exercise of his function of administering the provisions of the , and the Rules clearly include the power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute. [585C] 2.1 In view of the difference of opinion between the two learned Judges, the Letters Patent Appeal was referred to a Division Bench which heard the Letters patent Appeal and Civil Appeal No. 2611/81. The judgment of the Single Judge dismissing the writ petition is set aside. [584D E] 1.2 The order passed in C.M.P. No. 454 of 1981 is quashed and the appeal is allowed.

The appellants were displaced persons. They applied to the Custodian for a lease of their lands under section 12 of the (XXXI of 1950) on the terms and conditions set out therein, but they failed to do so. The Custodian issued a notice to the appellants under section 13(1) of the Act, as evacuee property, and under section 8(1), they became vested in the respondent as the Custodian. On the question whether the Custodian had power under section 11 to cancel the lease granted by him, HELD : (i) The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice in terms of section 12, and therefore, the appellants were not entitled to any relief under section 10(1). [982 G] Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, ; , followed. (ii) The Custodian had no authority under section 981 to cancel a lease granted to the appellant by himself and not by the evacuee. But that question was no longer open to argument as there has been subsequent to the decision of the Court below legislation which concludes the matter. [983 C] As suing Kumar Ghosh v Arabinda Mukherjee, , followed, (iii) The power under article 133(1)(b) is discretionary and absolute and does not extend to any other law for the time being in force. This provision is obviously intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 does not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and cannot prevail as against them and has been inserted ex abundanti cautela. [ 983 G] (iv) The provisions of section 10 are intended to protect the interest of the appellants if any other than those arising out of the lease, are left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities and that nothing in this decision should be taken as a pronouncement on those rights.

The appellant was a minor son of Raghubir Singh. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 5th May 1976 determined the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh. On appeal by the respondent, the Revenue Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer and remanded the case to the Sub divisional Officer, who by his orders dated 6th September 1976 held that Surendrapal singh was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March 1963 and was only 13 years when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisnt. Hanumangpur, and remanded it to the sub Divisional Officer for fresh determination of the ceiling areas. The Board of Revenue set aside its order dated 6 th September 1976 and remanded back the case. The appellant filed a revision application under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 before the Board of Reve nue, which was dismissed by the Board on 3rd June 1976. In the second writ petition it was urged that the Board had appellate jurisdiction and it could not set aside that part of the sub divisional officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. The High Court upheld the order. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board had by its order dt. 14th April 1975 directed that the ceiling, area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to new law i e.e., Act of 1954. [724G] 2.2 In the Government of India Act, 1935 there was provision under section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts ' but sub division is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Board over subordinate revenue courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to the Board to exercise its powers of superintendence on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of the subordinate courts so that to keep within their exclusive spheres of juris diction. [700A B] 2:3 The Board has general power of superintendence over all revenue courts. It is both administrative as well judicial powers. It was neither administrative as also judicial powers nor it had jurisdiction to make use of its powers. [624B C] 3.1 In the instant case, the Board has by its orders dated 14th 4 1975 directed the ceiling Area, may be fixed according to the old law. The order of Sub Divisional Magistrate provided that it comes to the conclusion that interest of justice requires exercise of such powers. The power of general superintendence and control over all Revenue Courts is both judicial as well as judicial powers and it was neither an administrative or judicial power. [774C D] 2 :3 In the present case, there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Act of 1956. Thus there was a provision under Section 224 for supervision by the State courts. The provisions of section 224 of the Government Act of 1935 were not subject to the other provisions of the Land Revenue Act. [764E F] 2(a) Under Section 107 of the Govt. of India, 1955 there was power of supervision and control vested in the Board. It does not vest any power of control on the Board and it does not invest any power or superintendence on the board. [750F G] (b) The High Courts have power to interfere with the judicial orders of courts. Reference may be made to Parmessar Singh vs Kailaspati AIR 1916 Pat 292, referred to.

The first respondent, a newspaper establishment, published a news or other periodical work containing public comments on public news. The appellant, an newspaper establishment in which the said law reports were published, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur calling upon it to implement the orders of the Central Government on the basis of the award of the Palekar Tribunal. The High Court accepted the plea of the first respondent and declared that the law reports are not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Dy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him was without any individual notice by the Tribunal before it passed its award. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that the Law reports published by the first respon dent were not newspapers as defined in the Act; and (ii) that no law reports published in the law books of the Ist respondent contain information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are supplied to it by its agents appointed at New Delhi and other places where High Courts are situated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports of the 1st respondent contain Information about the latest legal position prevailing in the country on any question decided in the said reports. [785C] 2.1 The law Reports published by Ist respondent are newspapers within meaning of the expression 'newspaper ' as defined under the Act. All India Reporter Association, Editorial note at the commencement of the decisions printed therein and also comments on some of the recent decisions of the Supreme court of India and of the High courts are almost as important statutes, rules and regulations passed by the competent legislatures and other bodies since they affect the public generally. It is well known that the decisions of this Court are almostas important statutes and rules, as statutes, Rules and regulations pass by the Competent legislatures and others since they affects the public good generally. [783E F] 2(a) The law report published by first res pondent contains information about recent events. News which have took place in this Court or the High ' Courts which were supplied to them by its agent appointed at the New Delhi, and other place where High courts were situated. It cannot be disputed that these decisions are of public importance.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th February, 1966 a fresh document of that date was executed and it was alleged that the appellant continued by virtue of that agreement. It was alleged in the plaint that the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. The appellant had been described as the licensee 'slicensor ' and the appellant had agreed to allow him to use the premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st August, 1970. The respondent filed an ejectment proceeding against one Sugrabhai Mohammed Husain and obtained a decree. It is alleged that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent desired to charge only more rent. Sugrabai Mohammed Husain had adopted ejectment proceedings against Sugraibhai Mohammed Husain. The trial Judge passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered eviction of the appellant from the premises. On appeal, the High Court held that the order of eviction was not put an end to by the appellant and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st January, 1975. Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High court had jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition in this case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court should not have exercised jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [1068C] 2.1 In view of the fact that the appell lant had been carrying on business for some time, it was a licence and not a lease. [1169E F] 2:2. The agreement dated February 1, 1973 was an agreement for leave and licence and the respondent was a tenant of Sugrabhbhai Mohammed Hussain and obtained decree. In the light of the legal position and also the fact, that the rent, light bill stood in the name of the respondent showing that there was no desire to create any lease by the document mentioned hereinbefore and the appe lant regarded him as a mere licensee. There was no error of fact as such on this point. [11069G H] 2(a) The agreement clearly showed that there were no desire or intention to create a lease by it. Clause (12) is significant which gave to the licensor right to enter upon the premises and inspect the same at any time. In setting out the terms of the agreement, emphasis has been supplied to the relevant clauses to highlight the points in controversy. [1016C] (b) The distinction between leave and license has been well summarised in Halsbury 's Laws of England Fourth Edition Volume 27 page 13.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before merger of former Dhol Pur jainpur State into the Matsya Union. The United State of Rajasthan became the Part B State of Dholpur in 1947. Thereafter, the United State Of Rajasthan merged with the Matsaya Union. In 1948, the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. The respondent claimed refund of this amount on the ground that the reason why he failed to export the entire quantity of the commodity before December 2, 1947 was due to market conditions and inability to get allotment of railway wagons. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the liability of the State of Rajabpur was not discharged by the State as it emerged on January 26, 1950 when the Constitution came into force. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The respondent could derive no assistance from the case of Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills Ltd., vs Union of India [1959] S.C.R. 729 and Maharaja Shree Krishnaid Mill Limited vs Union Of India ; , relied on. (ii)The State of Pepsu was not bound by any liability which might have arisen against it by virtue of the continuance of the old laws and the liabilities arising there under or even otherwise provided the law so made was within the competence of the new State and after the Constitution coming into force it did not transgress the constitutional limitations. Such a law must prevail and in the presence of such a law there can be no question of recognition by the Union of the right to exemption, if any, under the agreement with the Ruler of the erstwhile Jodhpur State. [184 E G] (iii)The respondent could not derive any assistance from section 3 of the Covenant which provided for excise duties. The right to claim refund was taken away by any law competently passed. Therefore, the appellant could derive the assistance of the case from section 5 of the covenant in the State 's competence to enact it. [185 E F] (iv)The agreement between the Ruler and the former jain Pur jaypur State was not an act of State and could not be treated as an interim Constitution. The rights arising under the old law were continued till they were repealed, altered or modified by the new state. Therefore the respondent could have no right to the claim refund.

The Madras Commercial Crops Act (Mad. XX of 1933) was passed to provide for the better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The Act was passed by providing for the regulation of the buying and sale of agricultural crops in Madras and also subject to certain other provisions of the Act as amended and the Rules framed thereunder. Section 3 of the Madras Commercial crop Markets Act (Madras Act XX of 1932) provided that after the establishment in such area of a market for the purchase and sale, of a notified commercial crop, no licence for the sale or sale of such commercial crops shall be granted or renewed in respect of any place situated within such distance from the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State Government. The appellants who were traders in cotton and groundnut who failed to take out licences on or before February 15, 1953, and threatening prosecution for failure to comply therewith filed applications under section 19(6) of the Tamil Nadu Commercial Crop Markets Act, 1933 (Mad XX of 1934) praying that they be prosecuted for breach of the provisions of section 5 of the said Act. The applications were dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the High Court held that section 5(4)(a) of Act was void to the extent it conferred on the Collector authority to refuse a licence at his own discretion and rule 37 was void in so far as it prohibited persons whose names had not yet been registered as buyers and sellers, from carrying on business in the notified area. On appeal by certificate: Held, that the provisions Of section 5 were not unreasonable restrictions on the appellants ' right to do business unless it was clearly established that the provision were too drastic, unnecessarily harsh and overreach the scope of the object to achieve which it is enacted. It was therefore necessary to scrutinise the provisions under the Act and the rules made thereunder to ascertain whether the restrictions imposed are reasonable. The question whether a particular payment is a trade allowance or not depends upon the facts of each case. Firstly, it must be a deduction in any transaction in respect o commercial crops. If it is a deduction out of the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, it would be a trade allowances. On the other hand if the payment is de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered, it will not be a 'trade allowance ' within the meaning of section 14 of the . The question of whether a certain payment is trade allowance and if so, whether the allowance is permitted to be received by the rules or bye laws framed under that section would depend upon the circumstances obtaining at the time the market is established.

The appellant was tried for the murder of one Ram chander Shelke. The Sessions Judge convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death under section 201 I. P.C., but on appeal, the High Court confirmed his conviction under section 304 Part II I.C.; but in appeal to this Court it was contended that the sentence of death should not be imposed because there were no specific charges against the appellant and that the circumstances showed that he had been guilty of murder and the injury on the throat was ascribed to him in the charge. Held, that the conviction must be maintained. The fact that the appellant was convicted under section 306 I.p.C, does not mean that he could not be convicted for the offence of murder but only when there are circumstances which justify the conclusion of a common intention. It requires a pre arranged plan because before a man can be vicariously convicted for an act of another, the act must have been done in furtherance of the common intention of all. There is then the necessary meeting of minds. The evidence that the injury caused was the one on the neck and there was nothing to connect this appellant with the murder is ascribed to the appellant in the absence of specific charge. The circumstances showed a clear intention to kill the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis. The mere fact that he did not want to enter a woman 's name does not by itself mean that it was not sufficient for the prosecution to prove that his separate blow was a fatal one.

The petitioner was born on 10.2.1922 and secured his first appointment as a Section Officer under the named employer on 22.10.1947. He was later promoted as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service with effect from 25.5.1954, and came to be confirmed as Section Officer by an order dated 8.10 1955. On 3.7.1961 he was further promoted as Executive Engineer, Class II service with retrospective effect from 5.11.1976. He challenged that order before the High Court in a writ petition filed by him challenging the orders of compulsory retirement and the Delhi High Court quashed the order of compulsory retire ment on the ground that it was passed without complying with the provisions of Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules as also the power to compulsorily retire a public servant had been upheld by this Court. The petitioner contended that he was holding an officiating appointment in Class II post when he was compulsorily retired and therefore, his case should be considered for promotion. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 56 (j)(1) of the Fundamental Rules is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis i.e. in a substantive capacity, i. e., in Class 11 service or post. The possibility of such incumbent being sent back to the substantive post is not at all relevant in the matter of exercising powers of compulsory retired retirement. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sation of superannuation is exercised, the Government Servant must be taken to be in Class 1 or Class II Service or post and he had entered into service before attaining the age of 35 years, and has attained the age o f 50 years. [642C D] 2. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to classify Gov ernment servants into two categories and sub clause (i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class III or Class I Service or Class 11 Service or posts. A person can be in class II service or Class III service or Post even when he holds a post of either class substantively or temporarily or on officiating basis. Instances are where officers are promoted to Class I or Class Il service or class II Service, or post even though they hold a post in Class 111 or ClassII service or posts, and they have entered into serv ice before attaining age of 50 years after the said servant attained the normal age of fifty years. The question is whether a Government servant officiating in Class l or Class 1 service or not can be compulsorily retired by exercising power under Rule 56 of Fundamental rules as also tho power to prematurely retire an employee in public interest and the classification of Government servants into three categories covered by sub clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) takes in within its ambit those Government servant who at that relevant time were in Class Il or Class l service or a post. [643B C] 3. The contention that the petitioner was holding a substantive appointment in class 11 service cannot be accepted. It is well settled that an officiating Government servant does not really belong to Class II or Class 111 service until he acquires a right thereon.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court for recovery of certain amounts due to the appellant Corporation. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the first premium was not only received by the Corporation completely on 11th January 1961 but it was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount was received by it without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality if any, the formality, if any. The High Court held that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11 January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the appellant corporation. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this case. [353B] 1.2 In view of the fact that principal amount together with interest amounting to about Rs 85,000/ had already been paid to the wife of the deceased, the Life Insurance Corporation does not insist on the full repayment of the sum paid and counsel on behalf of the Life insurance Corporation has stated that they would accept if half of what has been received by them, namely principal together with Interest amounting to Rs. 85, 000/ have already been paying to the husband of the appellant and his children, the life insurance Corporation in this ease does not insisting on the payment of first premium. Mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is acceptance not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [355C D] MacGillivray & Parkington Insurance Law, Seventh Edition page 94 at page 222 referred to. 1.3 The expression "underwriting and revivals" signifies liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. (See in this connection the Concise oxford Dictionary Sixth Edition p. 1267) it is true that normally the expression " tinderwrite" is used in Marine insurance but the expression used in Chapter III of the Financial powers of the Standing Order, 1960 dealing with the financial powers. [356E F] 1.(a) The dictionary meanings also indicates when the application so requires, the acceptance must be evidenced by the signature of one of the company 's executive officers. " Though in certain human relationships silence to a proposal might convey acceptance but in the case of insurance proposal silence does not denote consent and no binding contract arises until the person to whom an offer has been made accepts it unconditionally and communicates his acceptance to the person making the offer. Whether the final acceptance is that of the assured or insurers, however depends on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have progressed. [357F G] (b) The expression 'underwriting ' signifies liability ' under section 2(6). It means a mere execution of the contract in the mail. The test is not intention alone. When the application is so required, the accept must be communicated to the offeror, either directly or by some definite act, such as placing the contract In the mail, the test is neither intention alone nor.

The plaintiffs applied for a stay of the suit in which they were impleaded as defendants. The High Court granted an interim injunction restraining the Bank from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s V.S. Tractors Export, Moscow, (Thirt) and others. The plaintiffs applied to the High Court for an interim order restraining the bank from taking coercive steps in the suit. The application was dismissed by the trial court but the High court held that the order of ex parte communication was not a final order within the meaning of section 109(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure and refused to stay the suit as it raised the question of vires of the Bombay Prevention of Ex emption Act, 1949. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order refusing to grant an interim ex parte injunction was not final within the provisions of article 133(1)(a) and (b). The order declining to grant such an interim relief did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the Suit. [704 G] (2) The High court has rightly held that an order is final within section 109 of the Civil Procedure Code or section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, if it amounts to final decision on the rights of the party in dispute. [700 B C] (3) In the present case, the suit was filed by the plaintiffs for a declaration that the ex parte order of injunction was invalid. The trial court decided the issue against the appellants and the High COurt held that there was nothing in that judgment which supports the contention that this Court had departed from the principle of the earlier decisions or has suggested a different test for determining the finality of orders.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by the respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Act deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the amendment on the ground that by reason of section 14(4) of the amending Act, the Panchayat Samities had lost its power to appoint him as a Head Clerk and that he should be absorbed as a head clerk. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in service of the Panchayat until he was absorbed in Government service. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that by virtue of section 13(4), the Panchayat Secretaries were divested from their power under the authority of law, and since the appellant had been appointed as such on ad hoc basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis, his appointment as a Clerk prior to his absorption in Government Service had to be recognised and protected despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Acts came into force. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be consider ed for promotion but whether the Panchayat Secretary had the right to appoint the appellant to the post on ad interim basis or whether the panchayat Samiti had the power to do so. Clearly it had fortified that right on June 13. 1973 when it purported to do, in January 1974 on an ad hoc and in April, 1975 on an adhoc basis or on April 1, 1975. [737B C] 2. The appointment of the appellant as a sub clerk prior to her absorption in government service had to he recognised and saved despite the existence of section 33(4).

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math and the Mahant Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Yati was his chela of Mahant Shivshanker Yati. The suit was contested by the first defendant, who pleaded that on the death of Mahant, Shivshankar Yati, he was elected Mahant of Math Sauna temple and that Mahant Sadashiva Yati had been in possession as Mahant and Sarbarakar. It was claimed that in the event of Mahant Sadasiv Yati being found out of a decree for possession should be made. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yathi was not a regularly constituted Mahant of the Math, Sauna and that the Amauli properties must, therefore, be regarded as his personal property. On appeal by the plaintiffs, the High Court allowed both the appeals and held that the deity was a properly constituted Mahant and could not be considered as his own personal property and that it did not belong to the religious or the deity. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the properties in dispute constitute the personal property of Uma Shankar Yati and do not form part of the properties of the institution or of the deity, Sri Thakur, Gokarneswar Mahadeoji. [663C] In the present case, it is difficult to conclude from the material before this Court that the total income from the properties belonging to the Mahant and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan, deepdan, daily and annual puja and other obligations specified in the waqf deed. [665F] In view of the fact that the suit was not accepted by the assessing authority, and that position in regard to those properties taken in the assessment proceedings was adopted by the Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax, it could not, therefore be regarded that the entire income from these properties was shared by the Math or the idol.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. The Custodian General cancelled the allotment of land in favour of the appellants and allotted them to respondents 2 to 4. The appellants then moved the Deputy Custodian General under section 12(1) of the Evacuee Property Act, 1950 for the restoration of their quasi permanent allotment in the village Raikot. The Additional Custodian rejected the application on the ground that the appellants were entitled to allotment of suburban land. On appeal by special leave the appellants contended that r. 14(6) of Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour the appellants automatically stood cancelled and that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. Held: (i) The provisions of section 19(1)(a) of Act are not inconsistent with any other law for the time being in force, and they must prevail over the general provision. (ii) The words "subject to the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder" in section 19 of the 1954 Act are wide enough to cover cancellation only on certain specified grounds and therefore it cannot be said that section 19 (1) is completely in conflict with section 10 of the 1950 Act. (iii) The Custodian, by reason of divesting of the property, as from March 24, 1955, had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District expunged/Associate Regional Graduates in Girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (emale 's Branch). The advertisement inviting applica tion from eligible candidate was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was over on the basis of the results thereof. The candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry being over, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that there was improper feeding into the computa tion of some of the candidates who have better performance and in the viva voce test were not only called for. The State Public Service commission also decided to cancelled the entire selection examination and directed that the order of the Public Services Com mission cancelling the written examina tion would stand vacated. In lieu thereof, the results of the written exami nation were over. The Public Service Commissioner accordingly cancelled the written examinations and asked the candidates to secure lesser marks in the interview. The High Court upheld the action of the public service Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written test and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the examination, there was no justification for cancelling the viva pation of the examina tions and asking for fresh interview. [125E F] 1.2. The public Service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public would not suffer; public time would not had suffered; publictime would not be wasted in requiring re cruitment of what had already been done and the litigation could have been avoided. [126F G] 1:3. The Government has accepted the decision of the Uttar Pradesh State Public Services Commission to cancel/revoke the written Examination and asked it for a new interview of the eligible candidates.

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that the institution had two branches at the Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass as his Chela he was entitled to manage the properties of the Dera and the properties attached thereto. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that though the properties belonged to the Dasa at Patiala State, the interest which was the subject matter of the suit devolved upon him. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that after death of S Dass, the property which was subject matter o the suit had devolved upon Shiam Das as he was elected to be the Mahant of Dera. Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant. [489C] 2. The suit was for possession and management of the dera and properties appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be a de jure mahant against Som Dass as de jure muns since there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahant by election, that it was only when a person succeeded to the mahantship on the death Of a previous mahant, by election. It also applies if the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such a case the successor to the head in the mut tor or manager may be substituted as a party under this rule. [490E F] 3. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject of the dispute and the interest is the interest of the person entitled to the suit, but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest during the pendency of a suit, the suit may he continued against such person acquiring it with the permission of the court. [491F G] 4. The rule that has to be applied is based on the principle that trial of a case cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest in a subject matter matter of a litigation has devolved upon another during the pendancy of the litigation and the elected persons can be added as parties under Order 22, Rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [488B C] 5.
