The assessee purchased certain raw materials in the State without paying tax thereon, in view of the provisions contained in section 24(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessee sold these goods to dealers who, in turn, exported those goods out of India. On these facts it was claimed that the assessee is not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1). The claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the effect of section 5(3) of Act 1 of 1990 has been amended with retrospective effect from 27th May, 1971 a point of time when actually a prede cessor Act is in force; (ii) the amendment to section 9 (1) by Act 16 of 1986 is not relevant for our purposes and (iii) the amendments made by Act 44 of 1976 are not relevant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The purchases of raw materials by the assessees are not charge able to tax either u/s 9(i) or section 6 or section 24 (3). [364E] 2.1 The value of the purchases cannot be included within the definition of 'turnover ' and, consequently, section 6 will not come to the aid of the Revenue to support the levy of the impugned sales. [364F G] 2.(a) The purchase tax is leviable under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have to pay tax on them as well as purchases, the actual charge of tax under section 15 is only imposed on the sales and that part of their taxable turnover. To ascertain what this one has to turn out is whether the purchase is taxable at the point of sale or sale and the same transaction cannot be taxed as a sale in the hands of the dealer who sells to the assessees and as a purchase in the hand of the assessee. [365B C] 2(b) The value must, therefore, be included in the turnover, but the purchases are not liable for tax under Section 9(2). [366D E] 3.2 In the instant case, the purchases were made by the asses seeers as a result of the contract of sale entered into by them and they were registered dealers and furnished the declaration forms prescribed under section 24. Their sales were effected by the assessee subsequent to and independent of the sale made by him, then for the purpose of complying with, the agreement or order for or in relation to such export. [366E] 3(a) In the present case, there was no doubt that a tax is levied under the Haryana Act on goods in respect of which the purchase price was leviable under section 5 (1). But the value of purchases cannot, therefore be included. Under section 9 it is only an agent of the purchaser and the movement of the goods from the State consequent on a contract of Sale entered into with the purchaser would be one in the course of export within the meaning of section 2(p) of that Act. [367F G; 367A] (b) In view of section 9 of the Act, the purchase value of raw material by the assesses would be liable to tax under the provisions of section 6 itself even if the charge under section 10 fails. Explanation 6 inserted with retrospective operation from 27st May 1971 a ground of time which actually a dives tional sale is in operation and the assessee would only be an agent or purchaser of the raw material. [368E F] 4(a).

The appellants were registered dealers under section 11 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. In their return for turnover for the period from April 1, 1954 to March 31, 1955 they claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of certain transactions of cotton and castor oil sold by them. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim on the ground that these sales were made onroute basis and not on the presentation of the bill of lading. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of assessment and the notice of demand and the notices of demand. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The presumption in fu Contracts is that it is the duty of the buyer to obtain the necessary export licence. If at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate purchasing the dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sells to a person who is not a registered dealer, it cannot strictly be said that the declaration has not been carried out. [932 G] (ii) The words " a registered " in section 8(b) only mean a registered dealers to whom he sells the goods outside the State of Bombay. If such despatch is made by some person who was not a dealer, the certificate has not be complied with. It will be unreasonable to think that though the Legislature insisted that the certificate should declare the goods purchased were intended for being despatched by him or by a registered person to whom the certifying dealer had sold the goods, it could not strictly be held to have commenced until the ship has passed beyond the territorial waters of the country. [936 C D] (iii) The fact that the bill was retained by the sellers, the contract being that payment will be made on the presented of the Bill of lading and it was on the presenting of the bills of lading along with the invoices that the buyer paid the price. When the bill is made out as if the goods were shipped by the buyer, were actually obtained and retained by him, that fact itself would ordinarily indicate an intention of the Legislature to levy purchase tax on a person in section 10(b). [936 G H] (iv) The scheme of the legislature clearly shows nothing more than that the property in the goods shall pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the limits of India. The intention of parties is clear from the language of sections 8 and 10. [970 A B] (v) The intention declared has not to be carried out in the case of a notified contract until the goods are actually put on board is not disputed. It may very well be that if at the date a declaration is made, the purchasing dealer had his intention as indicated and ultimately sold to a registered consumer he cannot strictly say that it does not commence till the ship had passed beyond its territorial waters. [940 C] (vi) The rule in fu contracts is that the goods should be the property of the licensee at the point of time when they crossed this frontier. It is true that in the United Motor 's Case, 8th Edition, Vol. 4, 4 S.T.C. 133, it was held that the person to which he sells must be the owner of the goods and ultimately the purchaser should have been assessed to purchase tax under section 10 (b). But the fact that at any rate the export of thegoods cannot be considered to have started till the date of ship has gone beyond the period of territorial waters would not include the territorial limits.

The respondent divorced the appellant from her husband. The appellant filed a suit for maintenance and claimed that she was still a wife, while the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. The trial court held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her subsistence. The High Court dismissed the petition in revision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) section 125(4) would apply in the absence of mutual consent to live apart from moral and economic justice, a broader perception and appreciation of the facts and their bearing must govern the verdict not chopping little logic or tinkering with burden of proof; (ii) the respondent was entitled to the benefit of maintenance allowance and dissolution of the marriage made no difference to this right under the current Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available but here is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973 which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962 they entered into a contract to adjust their mutual rights; no settlement of claims which does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 125 can operate to nullify that claim. Nor can s127(3)(b) subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor cannot, not pro tanto but wholly. [79 E F] 2. The terms printed by section 127(3) (b) are manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the particu lar parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but pedantic purposeful. [81 G H] 3. The object of payment 'under any customary or personal law ' must be to obviate destitution of the statutory project can secure validation if the court is to pay true homage to the Constitution. The only construction of section 127 (3) is manifestly to recognize the substitute arrangement by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. No construction which leads to frustration of the constitutional scheme of the complex provisions in Chapter IX has a social purpose. [80 E F, 81 A] 4. Section 125(1)(b), does not require that Parliament intended divorcees should not derive double benefit. If the first payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 127, it cannot be said that the respondent has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree. Obviously he has no case of non neglect. His plea is not of non negligence. His right to ignore his right is to ignore. [82 E F; 83 A B] 5. Section 127(1) requires as a sine qua non for its application, neglect by neglect or husband. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The question must be clearly under stood that the scheme of complex provisions of Chapter IX had a social objective to protect women and children from moral & economic justice. [83 E F G] 6. Section 128(3), (b), is manifestly for recognise the substituted maintenance arrangement as a condition precedent for maintenance, but not wholly. The purpose of payment under any customary, personal or personal Law must be obviated by a formal exercise roasted in custom and no construction which lead to frustration would defeat the project.[83 E] 7. Section 129(3).

The appellant was a bidder for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month and the shop of Beni Country liquor shop held on 27.3.88. The bid of the appellant was accepted by the Collector on the ground that it had been given to the appellant in lieu of the shop being auctioned. The appellant challenged the order before the High Court which allowed the petition holding that the order of the Collector was not affected as there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was a requirement in Rule of giving prior notice to black listing an individual and that the appellant should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The black listing of the appel lant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have a right of hearing and making representation against the ord er. [869C] 2. In the instant case, the appellant had been afforded notice and an opportunity of making representation. The State Government will be at liberty to pass any order in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor. [ 869D] 3. The order directing that the appella nant be placed in the black list in respect thereof for future contracts under the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation of the bid of appellant is concerned, that is not affected. This order will not prevent the State Govern ment or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for ragging the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance law i.e. giving the appellant due notice and opportunity of being representation.

The appellant was the owner of a property. The respondent leased out the properties under two lease deeds in favour of M/s India Automobiles, which was then the sole proprietary concern of one of them selves, Gansdas Daskerdas Girdhardas (G) and his four sons. These co owners had leased out these properties under both the leases, what had been leased out to them was only a vacant land and that the superstructure had been built by them. They claimed that they were entitled to relief under the Madras City Tenants ' Protection Act and that their tenants were entitled for relief under section 10(2)(vii) of the Act read with the proviso to section 10 (1) of that Act. The Rent Controller accepted the contention and held that it was impossible to hold that the build ings, which admittedly belonged to the defendants and had been constructed by them on the vacant land taken on lease under exhibit P 1, ever were or could be the subject matter of the sale under exhibit 3 p. 1. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1)(a) The jurisdiction of the Rent Controller is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent Control Controller by the terms of the statute itself. When a petition under section 4 is filed, the Rent controller has no jurisdiction to entertain an application except by a landlord or a tenant, the question on which the jurisdiction conferred on it by the relevant statutes arises for deter mination by the Rent Court of Small Causes which has become final between the parties, is a total nullity which can be completely ignored. It was therefore not open to the High Court to entertain a collateral attack on the validity of binding nature or correctness of the order of the Court of small Causes and to consider and determine afresh the issue as to whether the L.I.C. was the landlord or not. [567 D E] (b) The question whether the appellant is a tenant in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P I, can be decided only on the basis of the rent fixed by the Controller. It will not be open to him to contend that the decision given by the Court Of Small Causes was not final between them.

The Mysore State Civil Service ( Integra tion) Rules 1960 provided for filing objections against the preliminary provisional inter state seniority list. The petitioner, whose date of birth is given as 28th June 1915, had retired from service on 31st March, 1954. He was given a rank in the final integration list and was still to be prepared after hearing objections. In the case of the petitioner, the Mysore State Public Services Integration Rules provided for filling objections against a preliminary provisional Inter State Seniority List and did not provide any provision for filing objection or appeal against the final inter state Seniority List as per Annexure 'B '. The respondent challenged the validity of the combined gradation list on the ground that it was premature as the final list of officers on an integrated seniority list was still t he final list was yet to be finalised after hearing objection. The High Court held that the combined seniority list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, was ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the Mysore Civil Services Integrate Rules provided only for filing an objection against the provisional Inter state Seniority list although he was given due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list, and that the concession in Shankariah 's case was confined to the facts of that particular ease. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The combined gradation lists dated April, 6,1962, so insofar as category 7 is concerned are ultra vires. [ 828 G] 2.1 It is not within the province of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. That falls within the purview of the statute concerned and the authorities charged with such duty. The power of the courts is only to see that an authority has acted properly according to the provisions of the Act. If that is established, the decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. [828 A B] 2(a) It is well settled that a Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the realm of the jurisdiction conferred on the administrative authority upon the character of rights of the rights affected, the scheme and policy of the statu tory provisions. The powers of the Court are only to ensure a fair and equitable treatment to officers in the matter of integration of services. [826 C D] (b) It must not only give an opportunity to the concerned officers to make representations but it must also give those representations a proper consideration. It is, therefore, not within tho province of courts to lay up what are principles to he adopted for pur pose of equation.[826 G H] 3.2 The power to the Courts is only in see that the authority has been properly according ly according to its provisions. If the established decision of authorities concerned would have to stands, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list.[826 C E] 4.3 In order to establish the invalidity of the final gradation list, on some grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. [827 A B]. P.K. Roy & Ors. vs Ram Chand & Ant., ; , referred to.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March 1979 was amended by Notification dated March 1979, which provided that the Additional Licences issued prior to 1st April 1988 would continue to be valid till the date of expiry and the Export House Trading House Certificate and an additional licence in terms of para 176 of the said policy. The petitioners submitted their application for registration as Export Houses and for grant of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licences. The respondents, however, rejected the applications of the petitioners on the view that they had failed to diversify their export of "other Products" during the year 1977 78. The said order refusing the Export Houses certificate was challenged by the petitioners in writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court which dismissed the same holding that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for grant or entitlement of an Export House and that there is no basis for classifying such Export Houses into two different categories on the basis of the date issuance of the Additional licences or on the ground of the additional Licences or on any other matters by order dated April 18, 1985 wherein it was observed that there were no requirement for diversification as a conditions for grant Of Export House Certificates in the Import & Exports Policy 1988 91. The High Court also directed the authorities to issue necessary Export House certificates for the year 1978 79.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at inter alia, in the State of Andhra Pradesh. It manufactures and sells fusel oil/Srenety Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the First Schedule to the Act. The appellant was a divisional McDepell & Company Ltd. It had its factory in the wholesale market at Visakhapatnam. There were two orders passed by the Assistant Collector one in relation to each of the aforesaid show cause notices, and the other by the appellant contending that as the drums were supplied by the buyer, value thereof could not be included in the assessable value of the fusel Oil/S supplant Monomers. The Assistant Collector included the value of drums in the value assessable of the said fusel oils/Sivam Monomy under Tariff item No.68 of the first Schedule to Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included for the assessable valuation of the goods, and accordingly, in addition to the aforesaid amount, according to the Collector (Appeals), it was not open to the Asstt. Collector to inflate the assessable values without establishing the receipt of the additional consideration by the appel lant apart from what had been shown in the invoice. The Tribunal also held that the appellant had not collected any amount in excess of the amount indicated in the price lists, and therefore, in adding to this amount, the cost of packing could be included only in the taxable value of such fuselons/Sinam Monoming. On further appeal by Revenue, the Tribunal held: (1) that at a time of the removal goods were deliver ed from the Factory packed condition, the containers being not returnable, and (2) that as per the price list, which were duly approved by the Asstt Collector, the appellant was shown the value thereof to be includ ing the value. On the other hand, on a correct interpretation of section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the costs of packing can be included, in computing the assessablevalue only when the packing is either manufactured by the asses see itself provided such drums/containers on payment of price in Civil Appeals Nos. 4339 of 1986 and 3941 of 1986 were delivered in tankers belonging to the assessee and only 10% of the sale was made in drums. In the instant case, there is no logic or reason for not excluding the value o f packing material supplied by a buyer himself which is of durable nature and returnable by him to the manufacturer. The "cost of such packing" referred in section 4 (4)(a) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 clearly excludes in these matters the question of its addition to price of goods recovered by the manufacturer and recovered from the buyer except where the packing was of duable nature and is returnable by a compen sioner.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Headclerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. The appellant was charged with having taken food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued the practice before the notice was issued. The prosecution case is that the appellant sent for PW 1 to the Police Station, who arranged a trap. As instructed PW 1, he was ready with ten rupees currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant. The trial court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and under section 336 read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court however, took the view that the evidence of PW 1 was insufficient to prove the guilt of the appel lant in view of the presumption arising under section 4(1) of ' the Prevention Of Corrup tion Act and that the conviction could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The explanation offered by the appellant was that PW 1 had returned the loan and that he had given the money for the Dipawali. The case of the prosecution is that PW I had returned it on the basis of a complaint received from the appellant that the food served in the Canteen was substand ing with the transaction of loan but payment of an advance of Rs 125 in the canteens when the appellant started to take food there. [337C D] 2. The evidence of PWs 1 and 6, the Principal, who had conducted the cholphintthaleins test with regard to the palm of the accused, as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled, is not supported by the evidence on record. It was also urged that the explanation offered was a true one. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution are not impressive. [336E F] 3. The presumption under section 5 (1) Prevention of ' Corruption Act is not attracted on the facts proved. Unless there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. [333F G] 4. The defence that PW 6 had returned a loan and had given it for the lakhawali was not accepted. It could not, therefore, be said that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant in view. [332G] 5. The conviction under section 16 I. P.C., is not sustainable on the proved facts. The fact that PW 3 had returned an amount of Rs. 125 in a canteen when the appe lant started to takes food there, cannot be any doubt that PW 4 was a qualified witness. He had thereafter received the amount of money from PW 1. The petitioner company was a public sector undertaking. The company had purchased a spacious flat being flat No. 151 Jolly Makeriary at 119 Cuffe Parade and the petitioner being the senior most executive was allotted the flat for his residence. In 1975, the company acquired a sp efficacious flat being no. 151 jolly Miderery at 119Cuffe Fortune in Bombay. The Company also purchased a flat being No. 152 JollyMakeriary in Jollymakeriary. In 1976, the petitioner instituted a suit against the company under section 630 of the Act in the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 37th Court Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat in question which had been given to him for his residential residence during the period of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 633 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the petitioner was a tenant of the disputed flat and therefore, could not be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company 's rules. The High Court also held that the provisions contained in section 630 were mandatory and therefore it was subject to a strict construction and there was no room for intendment. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the petitioner it was contended that: (i) the provision contained in s.630(1) is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to strict construction; (ii) the legislature never intended to include past officers and employees of a company within the ambit of section 630; and (iii) the words 'any such property ' occurring in cl. (b) refer to the whole object of enacting sub section (1) of section 6 which provides for prosecution of an officer or employee of a Company wrongfully withholds possession of such property during the course of his service, wrongfully withhold it after the termination of his appointment. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions contained by section 630 are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive. [175E] 2.1 The words ' any such property" in cl.(b) relate to any property of a public company as mentioned in clause (a) i.e., where an officer, or employee, of a private company wrongfully withhold possession of any property during his employment but wrongfully withhold them after the discharge of his duties. That appears to be one of the functions of cl. It would be rendered nugatory by cl. [176F] 2(i). The words "any such" in clause(b) are separated and by the words "Any such property", occurring in el.(a) refers to the entire object of the enacting sub s.(1)

The appellant, a private temple, was carrying on the business of offering Naivadya for the service of the sansthan. The temple was constructed in the year 1817 at Amalner and installed the aforesaid deity according to religious rites. He also acquired certain properties and the said temple with the said property constituted Shri Vithal Rukhamai Sansthan of Amaler. The appellant, therefore, filed an application under section 18 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 for a declaration that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The Charity Commissioner held that the appellant was a private religious endowment and not a private one. He accordingly dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the temple was dedicated for the Darshan of the deity and the appellant had no title to it. HELD: (1) The temple is intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public. [528 A] (2) The idol installed in the temple is meant for the worship of a family idol, it is a private and not ascertained individuals and the donee is a trustee accepting the gift on behalf. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public Trust in a given case. Even some of the tests laid down by this Court may be sufficient to enable the court to come to a conclusion about the character of the trust. [525 C] (3) The founder Sakharam Maharaj was a celibate and the successive disciples who succeeded as Adhikaris or the disciples were not owners of the property. This ancient document read as a whole does not admit of any other interpretation consistent with the nature of the properties and avowed object for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property had been dealt With or managed. [500 G H] (4) The appellant is not entitled to any declaration under section 6 of the Act as he was not an owner of the temple or a public religious endowment.

The appellant was a resident of India. He was prosecuted under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for the recovery of arrears of land revenue and for an order to enforce the same. The Assistant Collector attached the goodwill and tenancy rights in the said premises by a warrant of attachment issued on the 24th March 1954. The appellant 's application for the issue of a writ of habeas corpus was rejected by the High Court but eventually the High court dismissed it on the ground that the petition under article 226 was not maintainable as no application was made to the High Courts for the production and release of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The proviso to section 13(1) of the Act does not indicate a different and alternative mode of recovery of the certified amount of tax but only confers additional powers on the Collector for the better and more effective application of the only mode of recover ing the certified amounts of tax. [905 D] (ii) The power conferred on the Collec tor under section 46(2) is unfettered and unguided and enable the Collector to do so. But that power is not absolute but conditional. It is subject to a longer process of deten tion by putting pressure on the defaulter. In the present case, the classification has been made Statewise and it is clear that in the matter of payment of public demands of the States the people of different States are not similarly situated as those in Bombay who are a tenacious lot and must be subjected to a shorter process of detention by putting undue pressure on defaulter. [805 E G] (iii) The procedure for recovery of tax by virtue of section 46 (2) of Act 1876 is now removed, the vice of unconstitutionality is also removed and section 13 has been amended and the warrant of arrest was issued on 24th September 1954. [900 A B] (iv) The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and (v) that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. What is necessary is that there must be a nexus between the basis of classification and the object of the legislation under consideration. The respective contentions now put forward as to the validity or otherwise of section46(2), are unsound.

The appellant company was the workmen of the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents were the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The appellant company made a demand for a fixed recess of two hours ' normal duty, 2 hours ' and 12 hours ' at the Alexandra Docks. The Trustees apprehended that this was a device to get 4 hours ' overtime and rejected the demand. The General Workers Union made a claim for a fix ment of two hour 's duty, 3 hours ' duty, 4 hours " and 5 hours ' for rest. The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing system needed any modification. The High Court also held that there was no breach of the provisions of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest and that the rule of 10 hours ' shift into 8 hours ' work was not applicable as the corresponding provisions of section 55 of the Factories Act were not in terms. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that there could be no breach on the basis of the practice prevailing at the sawandra Cocks or in respect of the Flotilla Crew. [638 D] (ii) The provisions of sections 54, 55 and 56 are not as clear as the relevant provisions of them and they have led to long arguments before this Court. The scheme of the Act and the Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950, are not in consonance with section 13 or Rule 24. There is no provision in the Act corresponding to section 55 which lays down that the working day of an adult worker shall be so arranged that inclusive of intervals for rest it shall not spread over more than twelve hours on any day. The distinction between intervals of work and rest in sub rules (1) and (2) of Rule 24 is clear and this is clear from r. 24 which prescribes a normal working day ' of an individual can be so arrange that inclusive Of intervals of 8 hours and rest are not required to be spread over 10 1/2 hours. The only difference is that a worker must not be made to work for more than 5 hours at a stretch before he has had an interval for rest of 3 hours or fails to specify the remaining two hours as the case may be together with intervals of 6 hours in advance. [643 B C] (iii) The scheme Of the Minimum wages is almost the same as the cognate provisions of sub rules(1) & (2). There is clear antinomy between hours of work, and intervals for re rest. It means a break in the work during which a workman is neither called upon nor expected to work nor expectedto work. Having thus distinguished between period of work 'and the rest it is clear that on any single day the number of hours constituting a normal work is 9 hours. That number is inclusive of one or more specified intervals. There may be one interval of rest or there may be two interval of 8 days in advance, but the number for rest is not fixed to break up those hours. It is proverbial that time and tide do not wait for any man. Workers at a tidal dock work must be paid overtime.

The appellant tenant was let out on June 25, 1976. The rent was for a period of 10 years. The suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree and decreed the suit for ejectment on the ground that since the premises were let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1. 1976, the provisions of the Act referred to above will not apply for 10 years from October l, 1976, and therefore, the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act will not be available to the tenant. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that since during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court 10 years had elapsed, the tenant would be entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in section 20 of the East Punjab Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in this Act under Section 20 and the language of Section 39 and 40 of the is clear that if the provisions Of this Act apply then no suit for eviction can be instituted except on the grounds specified in the sub sections of this section. [164G H] 2.

On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the only power vested in civil courts in respect of ejectment suits against persons who sought to establish their rights as such. The High Court of Allahabad, in a writ petition filed by the respondents, directed that the pay scale of Rs.400 1540 to Section Officers and Private Secretaries should be revised and placed in the pay scales of Rs,500 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. The State Government accepted this recommendation and issued an order dated July 2, 1976. In a writ Petition filed by some of the respondents before the High Court, the appellants contended that (i) the pay commission was not on the basis of seniority alone but on the ground of selection by merit cum seniority; (ii) the fixation of pay scale was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution; (iii) the creation of two Grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretaries, who were doing the same or similar work is violative of the right to equality guaranteed under the Connstitution; and (iv) the High Courts have ignored the fact that vacancies in Upper Division Assistants/Lower Division Assistants are filled up by promotion from Routine Grade II. The respondents contended that Bench Secretaries Grade I should be given the pay Scale admissible to Bench Secretaries grade I with effect from October 1, 1975. The High Court accepted all these contentions and granted the relief prayed for. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) Bench Secretaries in the High court of Allahabad are entitled to pay scale admissible to Section officers; and, (2) The creation of one Grades with separate pay scales is violative by the right of equal pay for equal work. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification. It has a rational nexus with the object thereof. To hold otherwise would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. [303E] 2.1 In matters of employment of the Government of a socialist State must protect the weaker sections. It must be ensured that there is no exploitation of poor and ignorant. It is the duty of the State to see that there was no exploitation. The Court should not try toinker with such equivalence unless it is shown that it was made with extraneous consideration. [304F] 2:2. In matters relating to employment or appointments to any office under the State, these equality clauses of the constitution must mean something to every one. To the vast majority of the people the equality clauses have a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved. In service matters of the employment of Government of India, a socialisticist State should protect the larger weaker sections and it must be ensuring that there are no exploitation or privileged under the weaker section get their dues. Even if they have voluntarily accepted the employment on unequal terms, the State should not deny their basic rights of equal treatment. It was against this background that the principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has to be construed in the first place. Second, this principle has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. It had to be read into Article l4 of the Constitu tion. [305G H; 305A] 2(a) The classification made under the Rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of right to equal pay. [306B C] 3:2 The differentiation so made in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. The differentiation made in that cadre will amount to discriminatory treatment. The distinction made in this case is not particular to the present case.

The appellant Company was incorporated under the , a Central Act, 1956. The State Government decided to abolish octroi tax and to impose in its place a "tax on the entry of goods" which was introduced into the M.P. Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1976 (Act No. 23 of 1973). Section 69(d) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 empowers a municipal council to impose a tax payable by owners of buildings or lands situated within the limits of Municipality with reference to annual letting value of the house, building or land called property tax. The appellant company challenged the levy on the ground that no tax was leviable on its property since the Company was owned wholly by the Government of India and that respondent 1 was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the aforesaid two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(D) of M. P. Nagar Panchayat Act, 1960; and (ii) the power of taxation provided for in section 68(d), incorporated in its true signification any particular provision of the two earlier Acts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The tax is not in the nature of a fee. Apart from the fact that there is no data before this Court showing that the property taxes constituted an impediment in the achievement of the goals of the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, the provisions of the MP. Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 and the M P. Municipalities Act are supplemental to each other. [10688G] 2. The power conferred by the State Legislature on Special Area Development Authorities is a limited one. It is in pursuance of this power that the State legislature loses its competence to pass the impugned law. [688A B] 3. The legislative field covered by Entry 23, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution which says that "Local Government" shall have the powers which a Municipal Corporation or a Municipal Council has under the Madhya Nadu Municipalities Act 1956 or the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act 1961 is subject to four exceptions, one of which is that the principle will not apply to cases where the subsequent Act and the previous Act are supplementary to each another. [687F G] 4.

The appellant, who was the lessee of certain slate quarries in the erstwhile Hyderabad State, granted a lease for twenty years to the respondent. The Government of Andhra Pradesh granted another lease to the said Balumuri Nageswara Rao for a short period commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On December 10, 1947 the said Rajapuri Neighgeswara Rao leased out his right, title and interest under the said agreement dated January 10, 1942, to the appellant. The respondent applied to the Board of Revenue for renewal of the lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949. The Board of revenue refused to ratify the lease and terminated it under the powers delegated to it under r 47 of these Rules. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to forbear from terminating his leasehold right in the slate quarry quarries and from interfering with his possession and working of the slates quarries and other ancillary reliefs. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The lease was determined under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act on the footing that it is a valid piece of legislation and that its provisions do not offend section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935. [562 B C] (ii) The scheme of section 20 of the Act is to render ineffective all rights created after July 1, 1945, as against the Government without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the Government to avoid the same. In that sense the second Proviso would be a self contained proviso and the aid of the third proviso would be to a self operative one. [563 C] A.M.S. V.M & Co., ; , followed.
